Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. On July 13, 1960, at page 6215 of Hansard, during discussion of the estimates of the Minister of National Revenue, I said:
Granada T.V. network, which was mentioned earlier in dealing with the Ottawa application of the United Kingdom, is owned by Roy Thomson, who seems to be gobbling up everything in Canada, not only in the newspaper business but also in the radio and television fields. Therefore, if I am correct-and the minister may correct me if I am wrong-there appears to be 331 per cent of the capital of this company which comes from outside sources.
I have received a letter from Mr. K. R. Thomson, son of Roy Thomson, who in the second paragraph says:
I know that your statement in the house was made in good faith and for this reason I wanted you to know that there is no affiliation whatsoever between my father or any of his British enterprises and Granada.
Mr. Speaker, I made the statement in the House of Commons in good faith, upon reliable information. I regret if my statement has caused these people any embarrassment or if it has been unfair to them in any way. However, I feel that the minister responsible for the board of broadcast governors should inform himself and tell the house who is the owner of Granada.

speechtext:
I wish to deal with the question of a municipal incentive works program. The original announcement in this connection to inaugurate the matter was made by me on October 27, 1958; and covering, as it does, relationships between the two levels of government I now wish to advise that the municipal incentive program has in my opinion served its purpose well over the past two winters. It has provided tangible support, usually where most needed, to the overall winter employment educational efforts which have been steadily gaining momentum in all parts of the country. I think the house will have been pleased with the co-operation shown by all government agencies, provincial, municipal and federal, in carrying out this program in all the provinces.
During the past winter 860 municipalities participated, compared with nearly 700 during the first winter. While final figures are not available, it is estimated that over 51,000 men received on-site employment on some 2,600 individual projects involving close to 2 million man-days of work. These figures are also higher than those of the previous winter. It is not unreasonable to assume that at least an equal number of man-days were provided

indirectly in manufacturing and servicing material that went into these projects.
The total estimated expenditure on works projects undertaken during the period of last winter's program, namely from December to May inclusive, was $75 million as compared with $53 million the previous winter. Incentives have also been provided by several of the provinces which in total will involve additional contributions to the municipalities estimated at $4 million. Moreover, in some cases provincial assistance has been given to municipalities in securing the necessary funds to proceed with these projects.
Due to the results achieved in the experience of these past two years, and in response to requests from the provinces, municipalities and other bodies, the government has decided to continue the program during the coming winter and to extend it in a number of important respects.
During the past two years the classes of projects coming within the scope of the program have been broadly (a) the construction and major improvement of municipal roads, streets, sidewalks and bridges; (b) the construction and major improvement of municipal water and sewage facilities; (c) the construction and development of municipal parks and playgrounds. It is now proposed to considerably extend the range of this program, and in addition to the classes of projects already included the incentive payment of 50 per cent of the labour costs will be made applicable during the coming winter to the construction, major reconstruction, major alteration or renovation of municipal buildings, not, however, including school or hospitals, provided the federal incentive payment on new structures does not exceed $50,000 on each structure.
This extension I hope will encourage all municipalities with a backlog of needed projects to expand their winter works program substantially. The broadening of the program to include a wide range of municipal buildings should materially increase winter work particularly for building tradesmen, who regularly constitute a large proportion of the seasonally unemployed workers each winter, as well as for many workers engaged in the production of building supplies.
The second way in which the program is being broadened is to extend the incentive payment to a number of other projects previously excluded from the three main categories to which I referred earlier. The details of these are being sent to the provinces. They include such items as street lighting projects including traffic signals, municipal parking lots, water and sewage treatment plants,

pumping stations and water towers. In other major respects the program will remain the same.
I think I should add a word of appreciation for the co-operation of the provincial governments, municipalities and others who have made a contribution to the success of this important program. With its enlarged scope, an earlier announcement, and a continuation of the co-operation in the past I think we can be assured that the program will be increasingly effective during the coming winter.
My colleague the Minister of Public Works has already informed the house of the measures to be taken to increase financing for housing construction during September, October and November as a stimulus to winter employment. This together with the expanded municipal winter works program and the many other efforts of provincial and federal government departments and agencies in this field to step up winter work along with an over-all annual promotional campaign to increase winter employment will, I am sure, make a substantial impact on the employment problem this winter.
I should point out that in addition to this announcement the Minister of Labour has another announcement to make at this time, and that further projects and plans to meet the unemployment situation will be announced in due course.

Mr. Speaker, in accordance with our usages, of course, the Prime Minister has advised the house of the fact that the government is going to continue the winter works program, established some two years ago following a precedent that had previously existed.
The announcement made by the Prime Minister today, he says, has been encouraged by the fact that the federal government will meet with the provinces on Monday. We believe, too, that it was in answer to requests made from this side of the house during the course of this session in questions addressed to the Minister of Labour asking him to make an announcement of the government's intention with regard to anticipated unemployment in the coming autumn and winter.
The fact that the Prime Minister proposes to discuss this matter with the provinces suggests, of course, that the provinces have given an indication of their concern about the situation in the coming autumn and winter, and that the government believes the problem of unemployment is one that should be discussed.
The Prime Minister has not given us the full agenda of the conference but it may now be assumed, of course, that at the conference not only will fiscal matters be discussed but also 79951-0-4304

This is to be considered in the light of the statement of the Minister of Finance in answer to questions put, I think, by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, which indicated that there would be no proposals made by the federal government at all at this conference. Indeed, the Minister of Finance indicated that it was not to be a conference of that kind.
With regard to the program, the Prime Minister has announced certain extensions which will apply to certain municipal projects hitherto not included. There will be an opportunity to provide 50 per cent of the labour costs of renovation of municipal buildings, excluding hospitals, up to an amount of $50,000. The principle of the 50 per cent contribution is maintained, yet the Prime Minister will know that during this very session of parliament we have urged in speeches dealing with unemployment that there should be a modification of this program; that it should cover not only renovations, street lighting and municipal projects of that kind but others as well. We suggested that the program should be extended to a much wider area, to include, for instance, the cost of materials. However, in the announcement the Prime Minister has made the government is retaining the principle of a 50 per cent contribution, notwithstanding the fact that in many sections of our country where unemployment is greatest it is not open to the municipalities to provide this contribution, along with the provinces, because of the financial situation of so many of them.
Certainly the announcement made by the Prime Minister does not meet the request made to the government by the organization of mayors and municipalities in Canada. Having in mind the submissions made through Mr. Mooney, the secretary of that body, and the deliberations that were conducted in Chicago by the mayors of Canadian municipalities, the municipalities will not find in today's announcement a satisfactory confrontation of their requests.
The minister, in assessing the value of the program to date, has said that some 600 municipalities have participated and that some 2 million man-hours of work were created. One, of course, would ask the Prime Minister to indicate clearly whether or not the municipalities would have undertaken many of these projects in any event. This indicates the limited effectiveness of the winter works program as a means of taking care of unemployment in our country at a time when the numbers of unemployed are so great. Some 40,000 men have been put to work under this program at a time when,

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING TRAINING OF UNEMPLOYED WORKERS
speechtext:
I wish to make an announcement on the training of unemployed workers.
Training for unemployed workers has received greater attention over the past year in the house and throughout the country. I have welcomed this increased interest, as have other members of the house. Changes taking place in many of our industries demand more highly skilled workers, and it is
Labour Conditions
essential that many of those unemployed today receive additional training in order to fit into job opportunities on a continuing basis.
Over the past year or more the provinces were asked to provide additional training for unemployed persons, either by way of preemployed training or upgrading training, to improve qualifications in the occupation in which the person has been employed. In response to this request, stepped-up efforts to provide additional training facilities and programs for unemployed workers have been undertaken over recent months by a number of provinces. This has been done under our federal-provincial training agreements. The unemployment insurance commission last fall introduced changes covering the training of workers while in receipt of unemployment insurance.
As a means of stimulating still further training of unemployed workers throughout the country, the government has decided to increase its contribution in this field from 50 per cent to 75 per cent of the total cost. In order to encourage the provinces that have operated substantial training programs over the past years, as well as to stimulate such training in other provinces, it is proposed that the increased federal contribution will take effect when the volume of training given to unemployed workers by a province is above a minimum.
This minimum will be based upon the average annual number of days of training provided over the past four years as a percentage of the total adult population in those provinces which have had active training programs for such workers. When this minimum amount of training is given by a province, the higher rate of federal contribution will come into effect and will apply retroactively for all costs incurred in the training of unemployed workers during the fiscal year involved.
The details of this proposal are being communicated to the provinces.
In reaching its decision to increase the federal contribution to the provincial training programs of unemployed workers, the government has been strongly influenced by a recommendation of the vocational training advisory council. In this recommendation the council urged that the federal share of the training costs of unemployed workers be increased to encourage and enable an expansion in the scope of the training programs carried out by provincial governments.
The vocational training advisory council, I might add, is composed of representatives of provincial departments of education and

Labour Conditions
labour, and of national employer, union, veterans, women's and agricultural organizations. I might add that a review suggested by this council is now being made of the adequacy of existing facilities for training across the country.
It is my sincere hope that with this increased contribution to the training costs, those provinces which have been carrying on programs of training for unemployed workers will increase the volume of these programs substantially, and that those provinces which have not had programs in the past will now join with the other provinces and the federal government in actively developing and expanding this important and useful program of training.
It has been demonstrated many times in Canada and elsewhere, Mr. Speaker, that training is an avenue to steadier employment and to increased working and living standards. We must do all we can in the interests of individual workers, their families and the country as a whole to raise the level of our manpower skills. I am confident that the provincial governments and all members of the house share this conviction.
I fully expect there will be higher expenditures incurred for the training of unemployed workers, and provision for this purpose will have to be made in further supplementary estimates.

Mr. Speaker, the announcement made by the minister will, I am sure, find wide support throughout this house and in the country. One would hope that we could have a conference with the provinces more frequently, because apparently that particular event has succeeded in bringing to the attention of the government the serious problem of unemployment that exists in Canada.
It will be recalled that the hon. member for Trinity a year and a half ago in this house outlined in a rather memorable speech the desirability of an acceleration in our vocational training program. It will also be recalled that last February the Leader of the Opposition, when speaking on unemployment, referred to a recommendation which had been made by the vocational training advisory council last December complaining about the lack of progress made in vocational training in Canada.
The minister has now apparently decided to accept the recommendations made by this council, to some extent at any rate. He undoubtedly was also persuaded in the decision which has been announced this morning to take into account the observations of the chairman of the unemployment insurance commission, who said that only one in ten

of the unemployed workers in Canada was trained or skilled for jobs which were available.
This announcement by the government is very welcome indeed. It is a belated announcement and one which should have been made two years ago. It does not, however, fully meet the recommendations of the vocational training advisory council. It does not meet the recommendations made by the provincial governments who have asked for an increase in the federal contribution not from 50 per cent to 75 per cent, but have asked the federal government to bear the full cost in the light of its acknowledged constitutional responsibility in the matter of unemployment.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I can only say it is heartening that at long last, at the end of the session, the government is recognizing some of the recommendations which have been made by those of us in this party.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: COMMONWEALTH RELATIONS
subtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN COMMITTEE ON CONSTITUTIONAL DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I thank the Leader of the Opposition for giving me notice of this question. The answer is that such a meeting is taking place. The government is represented at this meeting, which opened on July 17 at Chequers, by Mr. Bryce, the clerk of the privy council.
The purpose of the meeting is to prepare a preliminary report for the consideration of commonwealth governments. Without going into the matters that are being discussed, I would refer the hon. gentleman to a discussion which took place in the House of Commons on May 16 last in which I pointed out that the present membership of the commonwealth will within the early or immediate future-and by that I mean a period of five or six years -conceivably be extended to 16 or 18. That
Inquiries of the Ministry would bring about tremendous questions; the question as to whether or not there will be equality of representation for all parts of the commonwealth; whether a country with a population of 300,000 or 400,000 will have equal rights at a commonwealth prime ministers' conference with a country such as India with a population of 450 million. What basis is there for commonwealth membership? Shall it be fixed on a basis of one million or two million people as a minimum population? Then there is the question of whether there should be such things as rotation of membership, as there is today in the security council, or regional groupings within the commonwealth, and the representation of such groups.
The reason for this committee of experts on the problems of the commonwealth being set up is to canvass all the possibilities and review the potentialities of the future, to the end that the commonwealth may not find itself stifled by anything in the nature of rules or regulations; so there may be preserved that informality which, as the hon. gentleman knows from his experience at these conferences, is so necessary if we are to maintain the commonwealth as we know it today. Without pacts, without agreements, without rules, we yet manage to bring about a general adherence to the maintenance of freedom everywhere in the world. To this end the committee now meeting near London has been set up.
I do not think any of the nations represented there have made formal suggestions or recommendations. This whole field is being canvassed, and out of the general discussions of these officials representing various parts of the commonwealth will come, we hope, something in the nature of particular suggestions which may form a basis for the determination of the future of the commonwealth.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: 265. Departmental administration, $986,595.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity of saying something in general about the work of the department. Along with other hon. members on this side we will have many questions to address to the minister when we come to discuss the separate items.
I should like to begin by associating myself with the tributes that have been paid to the members of the minister's department for their efficiency and devotion and the way they have carried on and are carrying on their duties. I do this with the greater pleasure because as the minister will know, some of the most valuable members of his department are graduates of the department over which I once had the honour to preside.
Perhaps the minister will allow me to say that in his own conduct as minister of the department he has certainly shown both energy and zeal. These are very desirable

attributes, especially in the conduct of this particular department. If we on this side feel as we have felt and perhaps still feel that at times the minister's enthusiasm and zeal have overrun his wisdom and judgment, that does not alter the fact that the minister has brought qualities of great energy and enthusiasm to the work of this important branch of the government.
This is, of course, a department of national development. If you like, it is the department of the vision. I would agree with what the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador said last night when he was speaking, that it is a great mistake on anybody's part, especially in a young country like Canada, to depreciate in any way the importance of vision in national development. It is especially foolish to depreciate the importance of development itself. Development must proceed in our country, of course in full co-operation with the provinces.
Our history has shown over the years that Canada cannot stand still, that she must develop. In this century we have already had three great periods of development, with inevitable pauses between. I think of the period from 1900 to 1914, the period from 1921 to 1930 and the period from 1945 to 1958. History, which is objective in these matters even though historians are not always so, will record the progress that has been made in these periods, and indeed in earlier periods in the nineteenth century when men of imagination and determination had the responsibility of implementing the vision of Canada's development. I am thinking of the opening of the west and the driving of the transcontinental railway over the prairies and through the mountains, a development that has always been associated, and quite rightly, with the name of Sir John A. Macdonald. Tributes have often been paid to him for what he did during those years to initiate and drive through this western surge of national expansion.
Perhaps some hon. members had an opportunity of reading in the last year the history of another great man of that period, George Brown, by the head of the history department of the University of Toronto, Professor Careless, in which he emphasized the interest energy and imagination shown by George Brown, the leader of the other party at that time, who at least in the early days of confederation worked with Sir John. Well, we pay our tribute both to zeal and to vision. Nevertheless, we have criticized in the past and we shall in the future, if the occasion for criticism arises, the exploitation and the exclusive appropriation of that vision by any group or any party. In these matters we also
Supply-Northern Affairs draw a contrast between vision and mirage, between development and declamation, between action and words.
It is quite clear from even a cursory examination of these estimates that exaggerated expressions of the vision are giving way or are being modified-which is probably a better way of putting it than "giving way"-by the harsh realities of budgetary considerations. Just look at the figures of expenditures in these estimates. As has been pointed out already, Mr. Chairman, there is a decrease of $10 million, and if my calculations are correct-and I am sure the minister will correct me if I am wrong-there is a decrease in expenditures in the north of something under $5 million. But more significant than this decrease itself is the reason for it as given by the minister, and the nature of the decrease. Administration costs are up; capital expenditures, employment-producing expenditures, development expenditures, if you like, are down. This is due, the minister told us last night, to the completion of several projects in northern Canada which were initiated by the previous government, certainly in most cases; and it is due to the postponement of other projects.
The reduction of expenditures, said the minister last night, "lies entirely in the construction field." He added, and I am quoting from his statement last night, this reduction is also "accounted for partially by budgetary reasons as well." I am not going to draw the inevitable inference that one could draw from this, that the other reductions are not due to budgetary consideration. If they are not due to budgetary consideration, perhaps the minister will tell us to what they are due.
Much attention has been directed to the development in the last three years of the work of this department, as was done in brief last night by the hon. member for Nickel Belt or the hon. member for Gloucester, or both comparing present appropriations with previous expenditures. Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, at this point I might interpolate to express what has already been said by other speakers, including the minister, my regret that our own member from Mackenzie River who is particularly concerned with the estimates of this department collapsed the other night with a heart attack and is not with us this morning. I know hon. members of the committee will be glad to learn that the report we received from him this morning is encouraging. I know hon. members will also agree that if he could only be persuaded not to come back to work in the House of Commons for a while he would be
6826	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs all right; but it is his indomitable determination to take his part in our work that has made it so difficult for him to recover from a previous serious illness.
The figures of expenditures by this department over the last five years, and I think the minister mentioned them in a very brief comparison are illuminating. During the last two years of the Liberal administration, from 1956 to 1958, two years during which we were responsible for expenditures, there was an increase in the northern affairs estimates of $24,863,554. In the first year of the Conservative administration, the year of the full effulgence of the vision, 1958-59, there was an increase in that one year of $24,527,180, almost equal to the increased expenditures of the previous two years. But the next year things began to fall off a bit, and the increase was $9,795,563. This year, as I have already pointed out, there is a decrease of $10,677,408.
That means, Mr. Chairman, that the dollar increase in expenditure on the work of development and in the work of this department in the northern areas in the three years of Conservative administration has been $23,645,335. The increase in expenditures of this kind in the last two years of the Liberal administration which preceded this administration was $24,863,544, or more than in the last three years. That should, I think, pretty effectively dispose of any suggestion that something new began in this field in 1958, and that nothing had been done in the years immediately preceding.
In any event, Mr. Chairman, the estimate show both in their reduction, in the nature of that reduction and the reason for it, that this vision is, if not dimming, at least less spasmodic and less oracular. The minister's statement confirmed that last night. The government and the minister are learning from one thing that development has to be related to the prior requirements of the depressed areas in this country which need redevelopment.
Every time I have talked about development, Mr. Chairman, I have emphasized that there are old, settled, well established areas in this country where development is even more important, important as may be the development of the new areas in the north. This development has to take the form of redevelopment. It certainly should not be overlooked in the excitement, in the significance and importance of extending our northern frontiers.
Then the government is also learning that development has to be related to needs and to markets, because so much of the product which results from new development has to


be sold abroad and there have to be markets for it abroad. Mr. H. D. Boyle of the Whitehorse Star, writing in the northern affairs bulletin some time ago on the slogan of vision, had this to say;
The only magic word in the north is "need". When the north's resources are needed badly enough, they will be removed, no matter how great the odds, just as was the first pitchblende from Great Bear lake and just as now the minerals from Ungava.
While we have to exploit needs and, if possible, create needs, I agree, of course, that we have also to develop resources which will make it possible for us to satisfy those needs. But very often, as I am sure the minister will agree, the needs that are developed-I am thinking of the need of foreign markets for those products which we cannot consume at home-can often be satisfied from our existing resources during the time we are looking for new resources which may be required in the future.
There is no better example of this than the oil and gas industry, which was mentioned last night by the hon. member for Calgary South. Great international corporations controlled outside of Canada move into our country, move into the Arctic, as they move all over the world looking for resources. They will explore, and then they will either leave or lease areas that they wish to leave or lease. If they do lease, and a good deal of this is going on in the north, in many cases they will relate the development of the area they lease, because of the nature of their operations and the nature of the product, not primarily to the needs of Canada or the Canadian market but to their own producing and marketing arrangements all over the world. That certainly constitutes a problem. It is the problem of ensuring that Canadian development will be based on Canadian interests for Canadian purposes under the maximum Canadian control.
Not very long ago the members of the present government thought this problem would not be too difficult to solve, but they are learning, it is obvious, the difficulty of reconciling the necessity of national control with the need of international investment. They are learning about the difficulty of reconciling the proper pace of development with the proper pattern of development. They are learning that it is not always easy to encourage Canadian investment in a way which will not discourage legitimate foreign investment. They are also learning that it is not always easy to determine exactly what is Canadian investment or Canadian development. The hon. member for Nickel Belt gave a very good example of that difficulty last night.

It was not many days ago in the house that the Secretary of State for External Affairs said there was no intention of intervening on behalf of a company whose property had been taken over in Cuba, a corporation which was registered, if only as a holding company, in Canada. But it was registered in Canada, and in that technical sense it certainly was a Canadian corporation. If it is not proper to intervene on behalf of a corporation of that kind which gets into that sort of difficulty with a foreign government, then it is going to be a little difficult to take credit for investments made by that company in Canada as Canadian investments.
Oil development in the Arctic islands area is a very good example of the possibilities and the difficulties of the kind of reconciliation which I have suggested is essential in terms of a healthy national development. Last April the minister issued oil and gas regulations. This was done after more than a year's study; after, so we are told, more than 20 cabinet meetings and after, so we are told, considering more than 27 proposals made to the cabinet by the department regarding Canadian participation.
The immediate result of the issue of these regulations was, of course, confusion. The minister himself admitted that these regulations were open to various interpretations. As he said at that time, "Any lawyer could tear holes in them", and he added, "We don't want to kill the golden goose". Perhaps he meant the oil goose, but he wanted to ensure that it would be a Canadian goose, and a very desirable preoccupation that is. He may not have killed this particular goose, but I wonder whether these regulations have not discouraged to some extent its desire to produce. The minister will probably deal with this matter when he replies. He will also probably deal with the criticism that he has not yet made this particular goose, Canadian.
What are the clauses in these regulations which were presumably designed to Cana-dianize the Arctic oil and gas industry without discouraging the necessary foreign capital, without which any vision of early development in that area could not be realized and would be merely another mirage? The important paragraphs of the regulations for this purpose were mentioned last night, but I should like to put them on the record now. One reads as follows:
No lease will be granted to an individual unless the minister of northern affairs is satisfied the lessee is a Canadian citizen and will be the beneficial owner of the interest that will be granted.
Another clause reads as follows:
As far as companies are concerned, the regulations require that oil companies to obtain a lease
Supply-Northern Affairs must be incorporated in Canada and must make their shares available to Canadians-[DOT]
"Make their shares available to Canadians".
-by listing on recognized Canadian stock exchanges or
Not "and" but "or".
-show that Canadian citizens are the beneficial owners of at least half the issued equity stock.
When it became clear that these paragraphs and other parts of the regulations were causing uncertainty and confusion the minister met the press and answered some questions, or he may have done it in writing. I am not sure how it was done; anyway, he accepted questions and gave answers designed to clear up some of the confusion. He dealt with the two points I have mentioned about Canadian ownership and beneficial ownership in this way. The question was asked:
What is the meaning of the words "that Canadians will have an opportunity of participating in the financing and ownership of the corporation" in section 32(3), and "participating in the beneficial ownership of the corporation" in section 42(5)
The answer given by the minister in an effort to clear up any difficulty or confusion with regard to this matter was as follows:
The department accepts the natural and nominal meaning of the phrases as applied to the particular circumstances of each company. It is impossible to say in advance precisely what would be required in any particular case.
I doubt very much whether the confusion has been cleared up by that kind of answer. It was interesting at that time to study the reaction of the industry to the regulations and to the minister's statements concerning them. There were those who said that the confusion and ambiguity in the regulations left them quite happy, in that it would make possible outside participation without too many difficulties being created because the regulations themselves were so ambiguous that this could be done. There were some Canadian companies, however, which expressed very great disappointment over the regulations. The Canadian petroleum association, which has a primary interest in this matter, of course, said they were consulted before the regulations were issued but that their views were largely ignored.
They strongly objected to some of the new regulations on the ground that they will discourage investment in oil and gas properties in the Northwest Territories. So, as the minister will recall, they asked for a meeting with the government at which they could formally present their views. It was as a result of that meeting that the minister sent them a clarifying statement and gave answers to certain questions.

Supply-Northern Affairs
There are many other questions to be asked on these regulations. We will do that when the individual items are before us.
Before I sit down I should like to say a word about one or two other phases of the work of the department. First I should like to deal with the questions of communication and transportation in the areas under the jurisdiction of the minister's department. I would mention first the Pine Point railway, which has already been referred to by hon. members on this side who have spoken previously. On February 12, 1958 the minister gave an assurance that this railway would be finished by 1961. In the speech from the throne on May 12, 1958 there was included this sentence, that parliament would be asked to authorize the construction of a railway to Great Slave lake. This was in May, 1958. At that time parliament was to have been asked to authorize the construction of a railway to Great Slave lake. We know what happened. A royal commission was appointed to examine the most practicable and best route. That royal commission reported in July of this year, 1960, without making any recommendation at all. The only person who apparently is confident as to what is going to happen is the hon. member for Peace River, who has stated-and this was put on the record last June 16-in the Edmonton Journal as follows:
There is every reason to believe the federal government will authorize construction of the Pine Point railway soon after the Manning commission report has been considered.
Against that optimistic prediction, which may be difficult to carry out in view of the report of the royal commission which makes no recommendation, there is a report in this morning's Globe and Mail by an Edmonton correspondent, and I wish the minister would comment on this when he replies:
It has been rumoured for some time that the federal government wants to shelve the project, once a sturdy timber in the Conservative roads to resources platform. A story from the capital last December quoted a key government source as saying giant new mineral discoveries in northern Quebec are likely to swing the emphasis on mining development to that area. "I wouldn't bet on Pine Point now or for some time to come," he said.
That is what is said of the railroad as to which in the speech from the throne in May, 1958 there was an assurance that money would be asked from parliament in order to begin its construction.
Then there is the question of highways in the north. Oh, Mr. Chairman, we heard a great deal about them in 1957 and 1958. We were given the vision of swiftly built Arctic roads opening up areas for development. However, the vision has now been dimmed by reality and by financial consideration. On


December 3, 1959, according to the Canadian Press, the Minister of Transport is reported as saying:
Mr. Hees found it necessary to explain many times that capital investment by the government for communications and transportation must go hand in hand with development.
That observation is, of course, a very sensible one. But it is quite a contrast to what the minister was saying at that time and earlier about the necessity of communications and transportation coming ahead of development. It is quite a contrast to the statements he used to make about the great program of works and roads in the Arctic as a contribution to the solution of the unemployment problem. When the minister speaks he might inform the committee how much employment has been given during the last year by work in the northern areas on communication and transportation. We recall that, with regard to employment, in the previous year about 2,300 jobs were created by this kind of activity, which in the elections of 1957 and 1958 was asserted to be a major feature in the government's attack on unemployment.
The estimates which are before us paint a gloomy picture about progress in communications and transportation. As to the Northwest Territories, the item for construction of roads and bridges is down by $2,800,000. As to the Yukon, the item for the construction of roads and bridges is down by $700,000. The item for national parks branch trunk highways is down by $2J million. All this means is that the Minister of Finance has put blinkers on this particular phase of the vision. Indeed, we predicted a couple of years ago that he would do so. The minister might be pardoned if, because of the activities of his colleague the Minister of Finance, he felt he was suffering at the present time from double vision.
Then the minister referred to the conservation conference called by the Prime Minister in February of 1958, and which we are told is now to meet in October, 1961 as a conference on "Resources for Tomorrow". We wish that conference well. It will certainly deal with fundamental questions connected with our national development. Like the hon. member for Port Arthur, who was speaking last night, I recall the conference on resources in 1920 which perhaps made a larger contribution to the parliamentary library, having regard to the number of reports that came out of it, than it made to any more concrete objectives.
I should not like to sit down without saying a word about tourism. We are all agreed now in this house and, indeed, I think in the country as a whole, on the importance of

tourism to the development, to our economy and to our income. I think we are all agreed on the effectiveness of the work being carried on, as it has been carried on for many years, by those Canadian officials who are responsible for encouraging tourists to come to Canada. No doubt when we reach this item we shall have some specific suggestions to make that might bear on that work. The figures on tourism given by the minister last night were depressing in the sense that they emphasize the imbalance between what we spend outside as tourists and what we receive in Canada from tourists, an imbalance which I think the minister said is not as great this year as it was previously but which is still substantial.

I suppose that figure can be accounted for in part by the difference between a week end motor trip in Canada and a two-month stay at a Miami hotel in Florida in the winter time. In any event, the over-all deficit in our tourist account last year, including our tourist account with the United States and with Europe, is now estimated at $200 million. That does not minimize the importance of tourism, but it emphasizes the necessity of doing everything we can to close the gap, just as it is necessary to close other gaps in our balance of payments.
I have dealt in a general way with a few of the items in the estimates, and when the time comes for detailed consideration of these special items I will have other questions to ask the minister.
Supply-Northern Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I would like to thank hon. members on both sides of the house for the very kind way they have treated the affairs of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources on the occasion of its estimates being before the committee. I think, too, that the one thing on which there is complete unanimity is that there is realization today of the importance of the tourist industry to Canada. It is not only important in the sense of the number of dollars which we bring into the country from this very valuable industry; it is also important to the mental and physical health of our own people.
I think, too, it is well that so many of the members of the committee appreciate the part the national parks play in this over-all recreational industry of Canada, as well as providing a place where people can go in this and future generations to find nature as it always has been.
I was very pleased to hear the number of constructive suggestions which were made in connection with historic sites. We are at a stage in our history where it behooves us to take every possible step to try to preserve these sites before they are lost. At the present time there are some 550 historic sites and monuments under the control of the department. Offhand I estimate there are probably twice that number of reasonably legitimate sites of national interest which could be added to this group. I hope hon. members will continue to make suggestions to the department, and we on our part will try to make the original investigations to establish the facts and put those facts before the historic sites and monuments board in the expectation that if a site is of national interest we can take steps to preserve it. I cannot promise, nor can any minister promise, that all the financial commitments necessary to preserve these sites will be made at once, but at least they will be put on a list with proper priority.
Having said that, there are two or three salient points which come out of the remarks of the various members of the committee concerning my department. One I would like to deal with in conjunction with the broader question of what has now become familiar, the term "vision". It has been pointed out, first by myself and then by various members of the official opposition, that the amounts of money included in the estimates this year for projects of a capital nature have declined, but that on the other hand the number of personnel in the department has increased.
The first argument which is put forward is, how is this possible? When you decrease your capital expenditures, normally you would

Supply-Northern Affairs expect, they say, a decrease in the personnel required to look after the affairs of the department. Another argument adduced from this decline in capital expenditures and this increase in administrative expenditures is that the vision has been lost, that it is fading, and various other phrases were used.
I want to thank the opposition for putting their opinions forward, I am sure in a very sincere fashion. This was proper criticism for them to make. However, I think it does bear out more than I can say the great loss we have suffered in that both the hon. member for Yukon and the hon. member for Mackenzie River are absent from the house at this time, because those two hon. members were familiar with what is going on in the area north of 60. They would have taken an altogether different approach, I am sure, and I want to put this forward in very candid fashion to the Leader of the Opposition.
If any person knows the history of expenditures under northern administration, which are the chief subject of criticism here, he would have known that the big capital expenditures which this government faced in connection with northern administration were for building a new town in the north called Inuvik. It was decided by the previous administration that the old town of Aklavik was unsuitable as an administrative town in the north to administer this vast territory. The expenditures for this new town, using very round figures, will amount to from $34 million to $35 million. These expenditures are just about completed. The hospital will be finished this year, and we have there in the north a new modern town the equal of any town of that size I would say, in any part of Canada, in fact far superior in many ways.
Like many other people coming into the department I had serious doubts as to the wisdom of making such tremendous expenditures for a single community in the north. Among many people from western Canada and around Edmonton in particular, who have made the odd trip down the Mackenzie river and have seen this development, there was wide talk of great waste and extravagance on the part of the previous administration. I kept my mind open and went up there last year, and part of my time I spent in the company of the hon. member for Mackenzie River. I went carefully and in detail over that series of buildings and the plans for operating that town, accompanied by engineers on the one hand and members of the treasury board on the other. After I made that trip I came outside and stated that, after careful consideration, this was good expenditure.


I make that point to the Leader of the Opposition to point out that since the government changed this department has carried the main load of these expenditures for this community. It was not a decision of this government; but speaking for my department and this government, I looked at the matter objectively and I made that statement, and there was reason for it.
When you see a group of empty buildings in an area almost a thousand miles from any other settlement it is a considerable shock. But I was there the day little Eskimo boys and girls came into the school, and I walked through the hostels and saw the way they were being housed and fed and looked after. I saw opportunity being given to 500 people from the trap lines and the fishing villages of our Arctic coast for education they would never get otherwise, because their families move around the Arctic area.
It is true that there are buildings and schools in each village, but much of the population still wanders and I think the greatest credit should go not to our department but to those Eskimo mothers and fathers who are asked if they wish their sons and daughters five years old and up to leave their homes and their families and go away for a period of nearly ten months to attend school and obtain an education. The parents of some 700 children were asked this question and the parents of over 400 children agreed. Theirs was a sacrifice because they knew that the only future for their children, since there is no chance of schooling for them on the trap lines or in the fishing boats, was to send them away and put them into the care of their fellow Canadians of a different colour.
I walked along the beach, along the river bank which some day will be beautiful, and saw the shack tents in which Eskimo families were living in Inuvik. The hon. member for Mackenzie River and I went into those shacks and spoke to the Eskimo mothers and some of the men. I wish the hon. member for Mackenzie River were here today, because if he were he would have asked me "How did you make out in giving these people proper homes?" I can now report to the committee that out of the 30 or more families who were on the beach last September, 23 families are now living in houses almost the same as many of the houses in which we live in Ottawa. They are buying their own houses out of wages they get through working at jobs in this community. Five more houses are needed to meet the waiting list, and I hope these can be provided before winter sets in.
This vindication of the building of Inuvik does not relieve the previous administration

of charges of waste and inefficiency. Because I have been fair about this matter of Inuvik 1 expect the opposition to be equally fair with me when I say there are examples of overplanning and waste in the north, and I know whereof I speak. I do not make much political capital out of this, because I can understand how in a new area mistakes can be made, and in our working out of the Frobisher Bay settlement, which presents a problem of a similar type, we have learned a lot from the mistakes made in the northern territories in the last few years, and I hope we shall not make the same mistakes again.
I should like now to go on to make a point which I believe to be paramount. I have explained how this peak of expenditure came about largely because of the project at Inuvik. The committee appears to have forgotten that it is the Department of Public Works which builds these communities, which builds these hostels to house 500 Eskimo people and children at Inuvik. But who has to put in the administrative officials, the teachers, the janitors, to run these communities? It is this department, and this is the year when these increases hit us, because it is the year when we are taking over.
I warned the committee last year that because of the ability of these Indian and Eskimo boys and girls to rise through the elementary grades we shall be faced with even greater expenditures in the future in order to provide them with high school education and the opportunities they need. The department will guarantee to these Eskimo and Indian boys and girls education to the highest level, up to the universities if they are capable of absorbing it.
As to this question of staffing, in the opinion of our department we have been looked on in the past as a type of Cinderella; understaffed, a junior department not worthy of the great dignity of the senior departments which have been here for many years. There has been a constant fight to get staff to carry out our task. Not long ago questions were asked of me in this chamber about starving Eskimos. We made expenditures on aircraft and so on, and to our knowledge there has been no case of starvation since the winter of 1958-59 when these terrible tragedies occurred. Therefore, when any hon. member raises in this committee the question of overstaffing of my department I get somewhat vehement, because I know the struggle there is in the department to try to staff these various projects that we have to carry out both in the general field and with regard to education, welfare and so on.
I have in my hand a series of simple figures which make this very clear. The expenditures of this department from 1954 up
Supply-Northern Affairs to the present time have increased by 245 per cent. During that time the staff has increased by 20 per cent. We have a large number of people on our staff whose overtime amounts to one third of their income, and that is not a healthy situation in any smooth-working department. If one considers the northern administration branch in particular, expenditures in the last four or five years have climbed by 539 per cent while the staff has increased by 195 per cent. This numerical increase of administrative personnel in the north has been long overdue and I would hope, now that I have put these facts before the committee, that the official opposition, which has used the figures in the estimates as a club to beat me with, will give friendly consideration to the problems we have to face in the north. I am very sorry indeed that the hon. member for Mackenzie River is not here to back me up in this fight.
Another point which has been raised has to do with what hon. members opposite have called the vision. The reduction in capital projects has been quoted as evidence that this is declining. Particular emphasis was placed on the subject of roads. I would like to put forward in this committee as emphatically, yet as quietly and objectively as I can, just what the situation is. This government believes in a system of private enterprise. This government believes it is not the responsibility of government to go into projects and replace private enterprise. We believe in what we call dynamic government as opposed to passive government. Dynamic government, to us, is simply doing those things which will encourage private enterprise to go in and develop our resources.
Let us look at the record. If hon. members will look at the departmental reports for the past three years they will find that revenue, just a few years ago, was dragging along at a level of between $1 million and $2 million a year. Every hon. member now has a copy of our last annual report, for 1958-59 and that report contains a statement of the revenue for that year. I shall not bother the committee with all the details; it is sufficient to say that the total is not $1 million or $2 million, but more than $12 million.
Where did this come from? There was an increase of half a million dollars from the parks, and I do admit trying to get the extra nickel here and there from the parks; we only get back 10 per cent of our costs from the parks each year. But the main bulk of

Supply-Northern Affairs the revenue comes from northern administration. Here is the break-down:
Branch administration in the north .. $ .3 million
Yukon Territory	 $1.8 million
Northwest Territories	 $7.5 million
Total	 $9.6 million
The total revenue from mining in the whole of the north was $252,000. From oil and gas it was $8.3 million and from lands, timber and grazing, $200,000.
Where did this extra $12 million come from? It did not come from the government. The government did not pay it into the revenues of the department. It came from private individuals who were going in and making deposits and paying certain fees to the government. When pieces of land were put up for sale they bid on those pieces of land. I am going to remind the opposition that this is just the beginning. There has been much said about the fact that in the Arctic islands individuals and corporations put their names down for 146 million acres of oil and gas land for exploration. When they had to put their money down only some 44 million to 45 million acres were taken up. The point is this; before 1958 whoever thought this area was worth a nickel? Not the oil companies. Not Canadians as a whole, and certainly not the Leader of the Opposition. He referred to this whole program of opening up the north as a program of building roads from igloo to igloo.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I know that the minister, who is being fair, would not want to misquote me. When I referred to that program as one of building roads from igloo to igloo I was speaking in terms of the employment that would be created.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not mind the correction, Mr. Chairman, because one of the fallacies under which the Leader of the Opposition labours is that he measures the amount of employment by the amount of money spent in the north, and that is not the way it works at all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is the way you measured it at the beginning.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That is a point I cannot accept, but I do not wish to go into that argument at this time. I simply point out the fact that two years ago no one across Canada thought these Arctic islands were worth a nickel. Today there are 44 million to 45 million acres of land out under permit for exploration on which deposits have been paid. They will have to spend $3 an acre to hold it for exploration; they will have to spend $3 an acre for exploration on the Arctic islands which two years ago in the opinion

of many were not worth a nickel. This will mean an expenditure of over $120 million that private industry will have to make in this country. That will be $120 million not spent by the Minister of Finance or any Canadian government agency but by private enterprise going in there to open up our resources.
To the hon. members for Nickel Belt and Gloucester who used a similar argument, and to the Leader of the Opposition, I recommend a magazine called Oil Week which published a special edition, reprinting from its previous issues in the period September 25, 1959 to March 12, 1960 significant articles dealing with this subject. I am just leafing through the magazine selecting portions at random to give an idea of the type of comment that has been made by the oil industry. Here is one article bearing the title:
25 to 100 Billion Bbls.
Oil in Arctic Islands-
Five giant structures could yield lour billion barrels claims Dome's exploration manager
The article follows. I might remind hon. gentlemen that these articles were written by people actively engaged in the oil industry. A subsequent article carries this caption:
Industry Looks North for Tomorrow's Oil-
The last oil frontier of North America covers more than 200 million acres in the Canadian far north-the Northwest Territories, the Yukon Territories and the Arctic islands.
A few years ago considered too remote to warrant active exploration, this vast area has now gripped the attention of the entire industry. Within the next decade oil men expect the far north country to be a major source of world oil production and reserves.
The article continues at greater length. Another extract from the same article reads:
Record prices for oil and gas rights in the Northwest Territories at federal government sales. At three Northwest Territories sales in 1959 a total of 3,764,221 acres were disposed of for $7,958,978, or an average price of $2.11 per acre, with a top bid of $8.26 per acre. Two years ago, Northwest Territories acreage was considered worth not much more than a nickel an acre.
As I thumb through these articles I find the same type of remark throughout. I could mention the transportation and scientific problems and how they are being met, but I believe I have made my case. This year and last-last year particularly-are important years in our history. Let me read the words of the president of one oil company:
A decade hence, 1959 may be recalled as an important year in the history of Canadian oil exploration. It was early in that 12-month period that private enterprise began its concerted drive to uncover the petroleum riches locked in the nation's northland. Though scientific findings are only now beginning to filter through, geologists are excited about the prospects. Much of the Arctic islands land mass is underlain by formations similar to those which produce oil in other

parts of the world. Modern transportation experts are finding themselves taxed to the utmost in an attempt to keep up with demands for faster, tougher, more reliable transportation across the rugged terrain.
I do not want to hold up the committee on my own estimates by quoting articles that substantiate what I think is a selfevident fact. Where the opposition has missed the point of what the government is trying to do is in trying to relate the expenditures of administration to expenditures for the development of this country. The first thing hon. members should appreciate is that private enterprise has gone in a way that would not have been thought possible until the Prime Minister made them aware of what was possible in this country.
I have not told the full story. These 44 million to 45 million acres are just on the Arctic islands. There are still another 70 million to 80 million acres under permit on the mainland. The total acreage can be held over the period of these permits if they do $3 worth of work, work that the government does not have to pay for because it is paid for by the oil industry. To hold the present acreage will require them to spend in the next 9 to 12 years the sum of $360 million or better. That is money the government does not have to spend in opening up the north. In addition to this sum the companies will have to make plans to spend from $30 million to $50 million each to prove up any pools they find.
When the opposition talk this way I wonder if they remember that last August there was an oil and gas find at Eagle Plain in the Yukon, almost at the Arctic circle. Do they remember that last February there was a new gas strike in Liard basin at Celibeta and that probably in the next year or so there will be a new gas line from that field leading down to Vancouver? Do they know that plans are almost complete for tungsten mining operations on the border of the Yukon and Northwest Territories? It is the hope of this company that in a year or two they will supply half the United States market and over half the United Kingdom market for tungsten.
Is the opposition aware that at this very moment the men who are up in the Arctic islands looking for gas and oil are busy, through another company, staking out claims on a very substantial new mineral deposit that they did not even know was there until they had walked around those islands looking for gas? This is how our country is going to develop. Sure enough, we as a government must do more to provide better maps, and the general type of exploration work that is carried on by the Department of Mines and
Supply-Northern Affairs Technical Surveys must continue and increase, but here we have the vindication of the faith of the Prime Minister and many other Canadians who believed that this great country had a great potential. The Prime Minister awakened this latent faith of Canadians in their country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, what has Canada being doing for the last 50 years?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
If the Leader of the Opposition were to get me started on an answer to that one he would regret it. In his own remarks today the hon. gentleman did something which was long overdue; he finally praised one of the few Liberals in Canada's history who have made a contribution in this area. The hon. gentleman praised George Brown for his part in the theory of the development of this country. If you go back and search the records of last year you will find a speech of mine in which I said that George Brown's contribution to the theory of development ranked with the greatest of any leader of this country. When I made that speech-I have the record right here-one of my hon. friends across the way made an interjection. I am sure he will remember the interjection he made and I do not want to press the point further, but to me George Brown had this philosophy. The other person I gave credit to in that speech was Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who picked up the Sifton approach to development and carried it forward.
But generally speaking, Mr. Chairman, I could make a fairly substantial case for the statement that in the last 50 years, to use the words of the Leader of the Opposition, Canada has been busy consolidating the development rush westward that was made in the previous century, and no one holds anyone particularly to blame for this because it was the normal procedure. But what we did was to relight the fires of development, in the rush to take advantage of what this country offered, in the hearts and minds of the Canadian people, and I do hope the Leader of the Opposition will give us credit for having done that. I do hope that after he has listened to what I have to say on how we brought this development on, he will realize it is not the dream of idealists; that these are the tangible facts we are producing to show that this development is going much faster than any group of people would have the right to expect.
My colleagues in the cabinet understood that this program of northern development would have a waiting period of seven to ten years before any activity would really come in, and we would have to be busy building roads, communications and airfields and doing

Supply-Northern Affairs all these things leading to scientific work to set the field tor private enterprise to come in behind us. But private enterprise did not wait; it just leaped right over top of us and now we are busy trying to improve the things they have at the present time.
This brings me to the point that I wanted to make when I started to speak. Something has been omitted, I think, in the explanation the government has offered when you find the Leader of the Opposition coming forward today and suggesting that development is needed in the settled areas of Canada, and not in the north.

I should like to point out that with respect to the development plan of the present government, 90 per cent of the money under the development plan goes into the settled areas of Canada at the present time, and I do not have to mention them to the committee. The roads to resources, for instance, are tied up with the settled areas as well as the resource areas of the north. This is a program that is costing the federal government-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I will wind up very quickly. The roads to resources program is on schedule. It will cost a total of $150 million, of which our share will be $75 million if Quebec comes in. I shall give the total rather than the details. The program objective for the roads to resources program as laid down by the provinces was that in 1958-59 they expected to spend $16,580,000; in 1959-60, $22,320,000; in 1960-61, this fiscal year, $20,550,000, for a total objective in the first three years of $59,450,000. Now, remember that these objectives are set out in the form of agreements, and when we sign

a contract after tender the contract sometimes runs for one, two or three years. Therefore it is very hard to relate these figures to the figures that appear in the estimates, because they are altogether different things.
Let us look at the actual expenditures. Here you have an objective for the first three years of $59,450,000. The total spent to date is $28,686,741. The total authorized to June 1, 1960, a little over a month ago, which includes the bulk of the provinces for 1960-61, is $40,778,009, or a total of all money spent and authorized to date of $69,284,750. Here you have a program with a schedule set by the provinces, estimated and aimed at $59 million in three years. Actually their program now calls for $69 million in the three years. Payment for these things may drag over three years, but my point is that the program is right on schedule, in fact a little bit ahead.
We have the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act in the maritimes. At the present time it is being used only in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Because they connected up the interprovincial grid system last year it was estimated that they saved over $20 million in capital expenditure. This has had the direct result of enabling those provinces to reduce the cost of power to industry in the two provinces. This is not an unsettled part of Canada. The program is also available to Newfoundland. We have offered to give the province of Newfoundland and the same thing for the Bay d'Espoir line to St. John's and another proposal has been put before me, namely the building of a line down the peninsula south of St. John's. This demonstrates that our development program is helping areas which need help.
Now about grid roads in the territories. I may say, to make it clear, that when I spoke of those grid roads in the territories our purpose was to carry out a program of delineation of resources, and this is where we were asking the provinces to join with us in building a series of roads from settled areas leading up to the north and into the territories north of the western provinces of Canada. We did our part. Besides paying 50 per cent of the cost of the roads in the provinces, we would pay 100 per cent of the cost of grid roads leading up through the promising mineral and oil areas of the northern territories.
The first push was through the Yukon, heading toward the Mackenzie river delta. That road last year was the first area we got moving into. It did not reach its objective. For the first time in living memory

it rained continuously in the Yukon. That is a desert area; they get only six or seven inches of rain a year, but last year it rained all the time. We did not meet our objective. This year the program is ahead of schedule and I think by the end of this year we shall not be too far away from catching up to where we hoped to be.
Now, these are bold adventures for our department, because it means building roads in areas that have never been considered before. I think we are carrying out this program in the Northwest Territories within the limits of common sense. We are building a road this year to Yellowknife. The people in Yellowknife do not think there is any slackening in the rush, because they are going to be able to drive their cars all around the lake and take them down to Edmonton and if necessary to Ottawa to complain to their members. This is evidence of progress. It is true-and the hon. member for Mackenzie River would have borne me out in this-that we were planning this year to construct the big loop around Great Slave lake to the great mining areas but on the advice of the officials of the department and myself we have changed to a more promising area.
I had a conversation with the hon. member for Mackenzie River, and he pointed out in an estimates speech last year that the money would be better spent at this time in putting it into airfields and communications for those mining companies. Those who were here will remember him having made that suggestion. I am sorry he is not here today to hear me give a report on the airfields we are building or planning to build for the mining companies. This program did not originate with the hon. member for Mackenzie River, and we did not take it ahead of time, but it made me conscious of the fact that we should advertise the program more. More companies have come in and will be coming in. For the first number of years the new tungsten operation will likely operate completely by air transport from the area at Flat creek down to Watson Lake. The concentrates will then be hauled from Watson Lake to Whitehorse, from there by rail to Skagway and thence by sea to Vancouver. Further processing will be done at Vancouver, and from that point the product will be distributed to world markets.
I mentioned that fact that in order to get more money for airfields and other purposes I held back on road construction this year and instead put more emphasis on surveys. The second reason for holding back this year was the gas strike in the Liard basin area. New wells were being drilled, and I had an idea that if the formation was good we might be called upon to build a road from
Supply-Northern Affairs Fort Simpson south to the British Columbia border. Therefore we had to spend more of our money on surveys. Surveying does not cost as much as construction.
I ask hon. members opposite who have had experience on the treasury benches to consider the position as I saw it. Here was a plan of grid roads for the north. It was our idea to build these roads and spend these millions over a period of ten years. But private enterprise does not wait for us to build these roads before it moves into these places and begins to press for roads in these areas. On the other hand, if it had not been for the rebuilding we did on the Canol road there would not have been the molybdenum discovery last summer which caused such interest, and which was found right beside the road. There would not have been the discovery of gas in the Liard basin if it had not been for the survey that was made there.
Perhaps I have made my points at too great length, but I have tried to put across as well as I could the arguments against the essential position taken by the opposition speakers. I would have liked to speak about Garibaldi park and seed grain advances.
