maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before this item carries I have a few questions I wish to put to the minister. I should like to put them now for one reason, so that I can go out and have some lunch and, second, so that his officials will have time to look up the points so the minister will be ready when we come to the details. The minister asked me last night if I was going to make a speech and I told him no. However, I said that was no firm commitment. Of course that was before the minister made this hour-long oration he has just made, which was very interesting and, I must say, much less partisan than the minister has been in previous sessions. On the whole I think perhaps that was a very good thing. I am going to try to emulate the minister.
I must say that if the minister will go back over the basic criticism of the vision that has been made by members of the Liberal party he will find that he seemed to imply that history had stopped at about 1900 and had only resumed when he was elected to parliament in 1957. There were some of us who realized that this represented a gap in his education, and it was therefore somewhat refreshing to have him admit candidly and
6836	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs very fairly today that the visionary decision made by the previous government, the execution of which was started by Mr. Lesage, to build this new town at the mouth of the Mackenzie which the minister described so feelingly this morning and which he agreed was thoroughly justified, was not a vision after 1957 but a vision of the previous government.
The minister said it was the Prime Minister of Canada who awakened the country to the importance of the north. I quite agree with him when he puts it that way, but I should like to recall to his mind that the prime minister to whom that reference should properly be made is Mr. St. Laurent. It was Mr. St. Laurent who, when I was secretary of the cabinet in 1952 and 1953, established the special cabinet committee on northern development which was the beginning of the concentration of all the federal services in the north. Incidentally, it was Mr. St. Laurent who, at the suggestion of Mr. Lesage after he became minister of resources and development, changed the name of the department to the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. Practically every project that the minister has been carrying out for the last three years, except the roads to resources which, after all, are not in the north or part of the road system in the north, is a project that was started in the past on the initiative and because of the vision of Mr. St. Laurent, Mr. Jean Lesage and Mr. Winters, with the support of their Liberal colleagues.
I say this merely because the minister for the first time since he became minister has recognized some of the things that were done before he came into the department and that he has been able to complete since. I know a good deal about the excellent foundation laid by the previous government. I will not embarrass anyone in the house or within its precincts by referring further to that, but without the excellent foundation and the splendid department which the minister inherited so much could not have been achieved by him. The minister referred to the department as the Cinderella department, but it has been no Cinderella and was no Cinderella when he took charge of it. Many of our colleagues thought it was the most favoured of all departments, but part of the reason it was so favoured was that it had a young dynamic minister, a minister whose dynamism is carried forward today in many other fields.
I refer, of course, to the present premier of Quebec, and I do so with particular gratitude because the present premier of Quebec was the essential person in realizing the vision that many of us connected with Newfoundland had, the vision that there must


be a national park in Newfoundland. If Mr. Lesage had not cut red tape at every turn and got that park established before the election of 1957 I must confess, non-partisan though I am trying to be, that I have some doubt whether it would have been established yet.
I just want to explain to hon. members what the establishment of Terra Nova park has meant to the province of Newfoundland.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: To Bonavista-Twillingate.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What it has meant to the hon. member for St. John's East. Without Terra Nova park the hon. member for St. John's East would not be able to drive his motor car, except for the crossing of the Cabot strait, from his own city of St. John's to Ottawa today. Terra Nova national park filled the gap in the road. Before the park was established three years ago it was not possible to drive from St. John's to Gander. That is possible today because of the vision of the previous administration and the cooperation of the government of Newfoundland, which has meant that a basic link in the road across Newfoundland which was missing, a basic link in the trans-Canada highway up to that time, has now been provided.

speechtext: How many miles out of the total?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The hon. member knows very well how many miles it is. It is approximately 26 miles out of the total. If the hon. member has not yet inspected that road he should, because when he does so he will see that it was a very difficult piece of road to build and that it went through a largely uninhabited area. Of course that was the reason it had not been built earlier.
I simply want to say that this is just one of many examples of the way in which, in the years before the present minister became minister of the department, there was vision, there was planning and there was development to which the minister has in one or two respects today paid tribute, which tribute I hope will continue from now on.
I must say that I also agree with what the minister said about the great reforms that have been made in the field of education in the north. I recall the day that Mr. Lesage came to me and suggested that my department, namely the department of Indian affairs, make an agreement with his department so there could be integrated schools for all kinds of children in the Northwest Territories. That was a vision, and it was not a vision after 1957, either. I am extremely happy that the minister has carried on that program and has established these good schools where Indians,

Eskimos and white children go to school together. However, it was started before the present government came into office.
When the minister talks about dynamic rather than a passive department and a dynamic government rather than a passive government, I think he is really overlooking history. As a matter of fact, notwithstanding the rather able defence the minister made of his administration, I think we cannot escape the conclusion that the minister's vision has been cut down sadly by the Minister of Finance's division.
I said, Mr. Chairman, that I was not going to make a speech, and I do not intend to do so. However, I want now to refer to the specific questions that I wish to ask, and I shall refer to them briefly. The minister has been good enough-and I want to give him great credit for this action-to further development of one of the roads in Terra Nova national park which connects the settlement of Terra Nova with the rest of Newfoundland. The minister is already aware of the fact that part of the road between Glover-town and Happy Adventure and Salvage passes through the park. It was surveyed last year with a view to its improvement this year. I may say that as a result of the building of other roads and particularly the main road in the park, the traffic over that Happy Adventure road has greatly increased. It is more than three times what it was three years ago. The road is narrow. It has many sharp turns, and it is extremely dangerous. It is also perhaps as beautiful a road as there is anywhere in the whole of Newfoundland.
I hope the minister will do everything he can to see that the work of improving this road is carried on as quickly as possible, and that in doing so the greatest possible care is taken to see that the wonderful views from that road are not lost in the reconstruction that is necessary here and there for the safety of the travelling public. It is not a long stretch of road. It is about a mile distant from the settlement of Traytown that the road enters the park and of course it comes out of the park before the settlement of Sandringham. My recollection is that it is perhaps five or six miles. Of course the basic road is there already. However, it is something that, from the tourist point of view and from the point of view of communications in the province, is part of the responsibilities connected with the park.
There is just one other thing that I am sure would interest the minister in this connection, and it is this. As a result of the establishment of the park and as a result of having a trans-island road, there has been an increase in the number of motor cars from
Supply-Northern Affairs outside the province. One day I just idly made a count of the motor cars that were going along the road, and every third car on that particular day was from outside Newfoundland. I remember that a few years ago one hardly saw any cars from outside Newfoundland. The minister need have no doubt that anything he does in the park to make it more attractive will be repaid, as it is in the other parks, by an increase in the tourist traffic, something which I know he has very much at heart and which he is trying so hard to promote.
I wanted also to ask the minister if, when he comes to the appropriate item, he will elaborate a little on a statement that was made by his colleague the Minister of National Revenue. The statement appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, of May 10, 1960. The minister will, of course, appreciate the significance of the date. The Minister of National Revenue is reported to have said as follows:
National revenue minister George Nowlan said here-
This was at Annapolis Royal.
-Monday night that the federal government planned to spend a large amount this year on the development of power between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
Mr. Nowlan was one of the guest speakers at the Annapolis West Progressive Conservative nominating convention which chose Charles T. LeBrun, Q.C., to run in the June 7 election.
I am not going to read the rest of it. However, I think the committee would be interested in knowing just what the plans are for these expenditures.
Then I wonder whether the minister can tell us about the road in northern Saskatchewan that the Prince Albert bridge was supposed to be a part of, as I understand it. I wonder whether the minister, when he comes to that item, could give us an explanation. I have here a clipping from the Leader-Post of April 1, 1960. The heading is '"Go Slow' Urged on North Road". Again, I do not intend to read the article, but I think the minister should tell us what really is developing there and what is the state of the road now of which the bridge was supposed to be an integral part.
The minister will recall that earlier in the session I took a great deal of interest in the Red river flood control development in Manitoba. I think we would all be interested-and I am sure the premier of Manitoba, who will be here on Monday, would also be greatly interested-if the minister could bring us up to date on the development of this project which, as the minister will recall, was so prominent in the affairs of Manitoba in a certain context only

Supply-Northern Affairs a short time ago. Can the minister at the same time tell us whether those parts of that project which had to do with the maintenance of the level of lake Manitoba and the possible diversion of part of the Assiniboine river into lake Manitoba, which was part of this whole Red river scheme, has now been turned over to his colleague the Minister of Agriculture to be dealt with under the prarie farm rehabilitation program?
I should also be personally rather interested, as I am sure would everyone from Manitoba, to know what progress is being made on the road north from Gypsumville to Grand Rapids, and whether it is anticipated that this road will eventually go right on to connect with the Hudson Bay railway.
Those are questions that I might not be in the committee to ask on the appropriate items when they are reached, and I should be grateful if the minister would answer them at that time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am sorry to be obliged to intervene again at this stage, Mr. Chairman, but the minister's statement requires some comment from me. I am not complaining in any sense about his approach to the problem or about what he said, but he definitely gave the impression that before his own advent to this department there had been what he called a passive approach or a passive government. Indeed, he specifically stated that there had been no indication from that side of the house when we were in power of the importance of developing northern resources, especially those of the Arctic islands.
I want to deal with these two points. I thought the minister was on the whole very fair and objective in his comments. He did ask us to bear in mind the fact that the reduction in expenditure this year is due largely to the fact that the work at Inuvik is almost completed, and that a great deal of money has been spent on that project. That is quite true, Mr. Chairman; but if you take that expenditure out of the estimates, and if you take that expenditure out of the estimates for the two year period before the minister came into office, I think the disparity between expenditure on other projects in the two years under the previous administration and in the three years since would be even greater than that which I mentioned a few minutes ago.
However, my main preoccupation is to convince the minister-but as the hon. member who has just spoken said, it is hard to convince him-that the work of northern development and the appreciation of the vision of northern development did not begin in 1957. Incidentally, the minister said that if


the hon. member for Mackenzie River had been in his seat he would have been glad to back him up. I am sure the hon. member for Mackenzie River and every other member of the house would back up the minister in every effort he is making to develop the northern areas. But I point out to the minister that the hon. member for Mackenzie River has had a good deal of discussion with the rest of us on this side as to what should be said on these estimates; and what was actually said, I can assure the minister, might well have been said by the hon. member himself had he been in his place.
So far as the importance of the development of the north and the Arctic is concerned, it is quite unfounded and wrong to suggest that this was not appreciated many years ago. Perhaps the minister will forgive me if I read some words of mine in 1953 which dealt with our vision at that time, the vision of those who were then in office. Incidentally, the figures do show that after these words of mine there was a steady implementation of that vision, as indeed there is an implementation going on at the present time. I said at that time, in 1953:
Within very recent years, however, the Canadian Arctic is being transformed from a vacuum to a frontier, and although it would be a bold man who would forecast the nature of its future development, of one thing we can be sure: if Horace Greeley were alive today, and if he were a Canadian, he would say, "Go north, young man!"
It takes more than a map, however, to give a picture of Canada's size. It takes the story of men with imagination, vision and devotion who have gone far, far "down north" to explore the mysteries of another world which, curiously enough, shares many problems with our own. Some of the men are explorers, who painstakingly map, not just the coast lines and mountain ranges which the aerial camera has already registered, but the nature of the rocks, the glaciers, the structure of the ice, the salinity of the sea, the minerals under the earth. Some are policemen, young constables of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who alone or in pairs have responsibility for the administration of law and order in areas far broader than many European countries. Some are prospectors, traders, missionaries and doctors. Some are air strip mechanics who, 2,000 miles back of beyond, have built airfields out of the gravel left by glaciers. Some are meteorological observers and radio operators who explore the weather from ground to upper atmosphere and send reports which will be recorded on every weather map in North America. Some are botanists, zoologists, seismologists; some cooks. They work in bitter cold under skies darkened half a year and on top of permafrost whose thickness man has just begun to measure. And some are members of our armed forces, learning to operate in this far northland. They have made camps to live and work in, aerial masts, roads and landing strips. Together they are opening a new land. In size, in problems, in ultimate rewards, it is one of the most challenging frontiers men have faced. It is important for Americans, as well as Canadians, to know more about it.

I talked at the same time, in 1953, about the development of the resources of this north land, and the variety of the resources and the importance they might have in the future, and I went on to say :
Overshadowing all developments In public interest is the search for oil.
And I talked about that search for oil in terms of the far north. I finished up by saying:
We know that there Is much to be gained from the Arctic. It may come in the form of power, oil, gas, minerals and general economic development providing the basis of new and growing communities. It may also come in the form of greater protection against aggression, for the north is a watching place for what may come from beyond the pole. Canadians have every reason to look to the north. We are now aware of its possibilities. Whatever the direction and emphasis of our activity, the Arctic is coming into its own; and, with it, new opportunities and new responsibilities for Canada.
Mr. Chairman, that was in 1953. In the recommendation made to the Gordon commission of 1955 by the department over which the minister now presides there was also reference to oil and petroleum products in the Arctic islands and to what had been done at that time to begin the process of exploration and ultimate development. Therefore all this was going on before the minister took office, and to say that development up to that time had been passive and that it all began in 1957 just simply is not an accurate statement of the facts. We all know what happened in those years. Development began in the earlier years and was continued steadily as financial considerations made it possible, and the minister is now beginning to understand what that means.
He has explained today how he has had to face budgetary considerations. So did we in earlier years. Development did begin then, and the department over which he now presides was created. There was a great deal of preliminary activity and the minister has carried it on, and so far as he has done that he deserves the support of all members of this committee from any party.
He talked, however, a few years ago about the vital importance of communications. And so they are important. But when we poured scorn on that electoral program of communications as the solution to the unemployment problem at that time, he interpreted that to mean that we had no awareness or understanding of the importance of communications at all. I ask the minister again, relating to this particular point, to let us know when he comes to this item how much employment has been given by the communications programs. The minister said that they have been reduced this year for budgetary reasons. That is understandable, but it 79951-0-431
Supply-Northern Affairs is also understandable that all this work began long before the minister took office and it will be continued long after the minister ceases to hold office.
There is one thing which the minister forgets. He talked about these two great areas of exploration for oil which are being opened up in an exciting way in the Arctic islands and in the north land. I think we appreciate the potential significance of that, and we will ask a lot of questions about it when we come to the item. But let me remind the minister of one thing. Most of this exploration is being carried on, in one form or another, under one guise or another, by great international oil corporations, and as I pointed out earlier they will conduct this development with their own international interests in mind.
We have surely learned in the last year the unwisdom, indeed the danger, of having our natural resources developed in a form which will make us dependent, when the development is completed, on international companies or on another government. We have learned about that in connection with the uranium industry, and we may learn more about it in connection with the oil and gas industry. While it is a fine and exciting thing and stirs our imagination to have this Arctic oil development taking place in the way the minister has indicated, let us not forget that it will be dust and ashes if we do not have the markets for the products of this development. And this is a time when we are having great difficulty in finding markets for the producing oil and gas wells we have in operation at the present time. If anything can be done by this government to ensure that this kind of development will not face that kind of danger in the future, then I am sure it will be supported by every member of the committee. But it is not going to be easy to reconcile these two things, national control and international investment.
That is all I want to say at this time. I do wish to try to convince the minister that while the work he has been doing during the last two or three years has aroused general interest, and while it has aroused our interest, and while I pay tribute, as I did before, to his zeal and energy, that work did not begin only in June, 1957.

Did the hon. member for Villeneuve ask about the trans-Canada picnic grounds?

speechtext: No, I just asked the minister if he would tell us how many miles of road were built under this program of roads to resources during the years 1958-59, 1959-60 and 1960-61. We would appreciate it if the minister could give this information by provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I wonder
whether the hon. member would be satisfied with the amounts spent, because it is almost impossible to get the actual mileage. Would the amounts of money serve?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The amounts would do.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That would be a big help to us. The total amount spent up to the end of 1959-60, with the claims in, comes to $28,506,741. That is up to the end


of last March. Would the hon. member be interested in what is authorized to the end of 1961?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I understand that it may be difficult to give the details right away, but could the minister not supply the committee with the mileage completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: This information could be provided to the hon. member, but I cannot provide it at this stage. Perhaps I could obtain it and give it to the hon. member after the estimates have been considered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I should like to thank the minister for the information he gave the committee about the road between Foleyet and Chapleau, but it puzzles me a bit. Two years ago the road was completed from Thessalon to Chapleau on the main C.P. line and also from Timmins to Foleyet on the main C.N.R. line, and a gap was left of 60 miles between Chapleau and Foleyet. Last year a 10-mile stretch of road was built on each end. I have not had the opportunity to inspect the 10 miles of road from Chapleau toward Foleyet but I have driven over the 10 miles from Foleyet toward Chapleau, and it is a good base road. This is easy country to build roads through; it is all sand hills, and it is just a matter of bulldozing a way through. Then all that is necessary is a good top finish.
The minister mentioned that 90 miles of road was involved in this agreement, and that would mean there would be 30 miles over and above the distance between Chapleau and Foleyet. I wonder whether the minister could tell us whether the extra 30 miles would be from Chapleau going toward Thessalon or whether it would be from Foleyet going toward Timmins. There seems to be an overrun here somewhere, because the distance, as I say, is only just over 60 miles, and 10 miles has already been constructed at either end.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On that same question did I understand the minister to say the road was being built from Timmins to Chapleau and then to Sault Ste Marie? Surely that cannot be correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
No, I was
paraphrasing the words of the hon. member for Timmins when he said in his question the road was being built from Chapleau to Foleyet. I gave the figure of 90 miles. I have just checked the record and find it should have been 60 which removes the difficulty.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
May I ask the minister about a road from Elliot Lake to Chapleau which has been discussed in connection with the effort that is being made to assist this community. Not long ago it was mentioned, I

think by the representative of the provincial government at Elliot Lake, that agreement had been reached to permit construction of this road. Can the minister say anything about that?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We have received no application yet from the province of Ontario to build this road under the program even though there is opportunity now under the total amount of $15 million for a road if it meets our criteria.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is the minister saying no request has been made by the government of the province of Ontario for an agreement to make possible the construction of this road under the program?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
As far as we
know here the answer I gave is correct. We have received no application but we may find something in the files. We could make a check on that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I would just like to call the minister's attention to statements that have come out of Queen's Park that the road has been agreed on and the work is to begin shortly. This has caused a good deal of interest in the community concerned.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Does the figure of $28 million cited a few moments ago by the minister represent the share of the federal government?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, that would be impossible because the total amount that can be spent in any one given year is limited. It varies every year. If the program were acted on at full speed, in five years it would be half or $15 million a year. Therefore, the figure we have given of $28 million for the amount actually spent to date covers part of 1958-59 and all of 1959-60 and part of this year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: So the federal government's share would be $14 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: If our share is $14 million for the work which has been approved now I do not know why the minister cannot say that this represents so many miles of road completed, so many miles of road cleared and so many miles gravelled. He must have that information. Surely we are not approving $14 million without knowing what has been done.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I will be glad to get that information for the hon. member. It requires looking at all the contracts for engineering, clearing, grading and so on. It requires a review of the whole series of operations involving many hours of work. However, we will be glad to get that information for 79951-0-431J
Supply-Northern Affairs the hon. member. If there is a particular road or province he wants us to concentrate on, we could, or does he want the full picture?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: : Yes. We are asked to approve a $14 million vote which was only $9 million last year and we do not have all the information we should have. The government should know what has been done to date with respect to the $14 million which represents quite a number of miles of road.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, last evening I made reference to a request made by the province of New Brunswick under this program for the approval of the construction of a bridge to link Shippegan island to Miscou island. The request was turned down by the department. I believe the reason as I mentioned last night was that there was not enough industry to be developed on Miscou island. In view of the new approach I made in my remarks would the minister feel that new representations might be given favourable consideration? There is one of the largest peat moss beds in eastern Canada located on Miscou island. If new representations were made by the province to his department stressing the importance of the development of the peat moss beds on Miscou island would the representations receive more favourable consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The previous administration in the province of New Brunswick, as the hon. member pointed out, made extremely strong representations to us about this bridge. They were turned down on the ground that it did not meet in full the criteria we set up. However, I am sending my assistant deputy minister on a visit next week to the new government of New Brunswick to discuss the whole roads to resources program with them and I am sure this matter will be discussed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Could the minister say whether in his discussions with the province of Quebec there was any discussion of any particular road which might have priority should Quebec come into the scheme? Is there one road which would have priority should Quebec come in?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the representatives of the previous administration in Quebec came to us and discussed a road from Amos up to Mattagami lake. We said we could not accept that as the first road under the agreement because they let a contract on that road without calling tenders. You will recall that Mr. Lesage who was then a member of this house took strong exception to doing anything with the province unless it was put out to tender. When

Supply-Northern Affairs the next administration came in the same question was raised with us and we were asked to reconsider our position. As I mentioned to the previous speaker my deputy is leaving this Wednesday to consult with the governments of the two new administrations to see what can be done to meet our conditions and criteria on this roads to resources program. We are anxious that the good feeling established with all governments across Canada be maintained with respect to this program.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: And the first road would be from Amos to where?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As I understand it, it starts at the southerly extremity of a town called Amos and moves northward to lake Mattagami where there is a base metal deposit of lead and zinc which is being brought into production. I will not say anything further about our discussions with the provincial administration but the request was turned down because they let a contract on that road without calling tenders.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Can the minister tell us the amount submitted by each province with respect to the $28 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Out of the $5,638,449 submitted by the province of Nova Scotia, as submitted by the minister, how many roads or projects are covered?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
In the case of the provinces of Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia where it was not possible to get roads to resources within the ambit of what we had originally announced, namely to open up new mining, forest and recreational areas, we allowed those two provinces to substitute tourist roads. In the case of Nova Scotia there are many such projects, some 16 in number, and the road pattern is already well established. It is simply a matter of bringing them up to tourist levels. I think

the same answer applies to the extensive program on Prince Edward Island; there are 31 in Prince Edward Island.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to return to a road under the roads to resources program, the proposed road out of Elliot Lake to Chapleau, and read to the minister what was said, I think it was two weeks ago last Sunday, by the minister of mines of the government of Ontario in Elliot Lake when he was speaking there. I quote from the text of his speech because it has a bearing on this program. He said:
We-
That is the government of Ontario.
-have closely studied the building of a road connecting Elliot Lake to the Chapleau highway and will press the federal government to give its approval to this project. We must have this approval before we can proceed, since the road would come under the federal-provincial roads to resources program.
What I want to ask the minister is whether the pressure which the provincial minister refers to has been brought to bear on the federal government, and what is the attitude of the federal government toward sharing in this particular program?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The only thing I can say is that I know of a good many things that the committee on helping out Elliot Lake and Uranium City have been discussing, and this is one. If it comes under the plans of my department, on which there has been no official approach made to the government to my knowledge, then I will be glad to consider it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have quite a number of questions on this particular item. There was an announcement in the Globe and Mail of December 23 that the pact was signed for these major projects, making a total of 335 mil pc of road, and that the termination date of all these agreements for these six roads is March 31, 1967. Does that mean, for example, that the Spruce river road, about 70 miles, starting at highway No. 17 at Port Arthur and running north to Cheeseman lake, has got a completion target date of 1967? I am especially interested in this particular road because, as the minister may know, there is a controversy in the areas about it. Part of the road has been under the control of one of the pulp and paper companies and free access to the area opened up by the road has not been allowed. I want to know particularly what is the position of the federal government in so far as these roads are concerned, or roads to which it contributes in so far as there being free access to the general public is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We are a little uncertain as to which road is being discussed. The hon. member mentioned Spruce lake.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Spruce river road.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We have a road in our program north of Port Arthur, about 70 miles long, which runs from the trans-Canada highway immediately east of Port Arthur, extending in a northerly direction to the vicinity of Cheeseman lake west.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The estimated cost of that road is $3 million, and we will find out what has been done. I did not recognize it under the designation of Spruce lake. Up to the end of last year 28 miles had been cleared at a cost of $560,572.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is this one of the roads toward which the Abitibi Pulp and Paper Company and other private companies are making contribution?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am informed that this is the road, yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Has the minister any say or control over the road, or can he tell me whether there is anything in the agreement that will provide for free access to the general public at all times for the full length of that road?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Any road that we participate in will be, as far as we are concerned, free to the public, free access, and if the hon. member is correct in his information I think the point should be inquired into. This one will be free to public use.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I just want to make sure it was part of the agreement because I can give an example of the type of problem that is coming up. We have this road of 50 miles planned to Nakina, to Cavell and to Durer lake, to tap the big iron ore project run by Anaconda. Anaconda, I gather-I do not want to malign the company-has certain views on union participation and union organization. It has already blocked entrance to its property by land to union organizers. The union organizers who have gone in have had to go in by plane to approach the rim of the property. If we have a situation where Anaconda is putting up part of the funds for this road and by so doing is able to control access into its property, in a situation such as this I think the minister can see that we have a potential controversy of large scale on our hands. I should like to know that the agreements contain an assurance that the total road program provides for free access and that that is part of the agreement, part of the understanding or undertaking given by the
Supply-Northern Affairs federal government. This may seem like a small point but I think it is potential dynamite. The minister may remember the bad feeling we have had in northwestern Ontario over access to pulp and paper company roads. I know pulp and paper companies have to be careful about the protection of their workers from hunters and of their limits from the possibilities of fire, but surely if the federal government is putting money into roads there should be no question at all about public access. I should like to have that assurance from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I can give the hon. member that assurance with every enthusiasm.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I have from the minister just how much Abitibi is contributing to that particular Spruce river road to Cheese-man lake north?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The proportion is always one third if there is a private enterprise company mixed up in the building of a road.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Let me turn to what this story says:
The major project under the agreement is yet to come. It will consist of a road or roads into the northwestern part of the province with a southern terminus on or north of the C.N.H. main line and somewhere in the area between Nakina and the Manitoba boundary. The exact locations will be determined by the results of an aeromagnetic survey and the subsequent necessary geological ground reconnaissance.
I should like to know more about this. As the minister knows, Nakina is one of those threefold divisional points of the C.N.R. In other words, there are about 400 miles between the Manitoba boundary and Nakina and to say that the southern terminus is going to be somewhere between Nakina and the Manitoba boundary is about as indefinite as one can get. I should like to know more about the project and whether anything further has developed with regard to it. This is supposed to be a major project and I think we are entitled to have more indication of what is involved. Is it planned to hook up with the Pickle lake area and the road which is already contemplated between Goldpines and Uchi lake and to have a road run over to Red Lake or from the Red Lake road over to Pickle lake or down to Goldpines and Uchi lake and then up to Pickle lake? There is a great deal of interest in this matter and I hope the minister can give us more details.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The explanation of this is that during our negotiations with the province of Ontario they put forward a program they have been carrying

Supply-Northern Affairs on for a number of years involving the connecting of areas on one railway line with areas on the other railway line and at the same time opening up resources of various types. We on our part put forward the point of view that this would be satisfactory to us but we hoped that the province of Ontario would take a look at the mineral possibilities and the pulp and paper possibilities of a great area of northwestern Ontario that at the present time is not opened up either by rail or by road.
The Ontario government took the attitude, I think rightly and soundly, that before they embarked on a venture of opening up such a vast area they would have to know a great deal more about it. Therefore a joint program involving the federal government and the provincial government was undertaken through another department to do an aerial magnetometer survey of the whole area west from Nakina to the Manitoba border. This big venture is still going on. In addition to the aerial magnetometer survey there would also be a ground survey involving geological teams going in to look at some of the more interesting anomalies.
I understand that at the present time a series of maps has been prepared and published covering this area. When the aerial and ground work is finished the two governments will then sit down and on the basis of what we know about resources, more than we now know, will try to plot a road that will give closer access to the most promising portions of this area. As a sidelight to my reply, if you like, I happened to be on a C.N.R. train the day after the first map was published and found myself in the middle of a rush of prospectors who had got the map in Toronto and were heading out to Armstrong the next day. I know how quickly there is a reaction in the prospecting and mining industry when information of this type is published. It is the making of information of this type available that will lead to the opening up of our country much more quickly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The unsatisfactory part of the minister's explanation is this. From the minister's experience in living in Kenora and knowing the situation north of there, north of Sioux Lookout and north of the C.N.R. line generally, he will probably know that there has been certain disgruntlement on the part of the forestry people, especially the pulp and paper companies, over the alacrity with which the provincial government moves to provide roads for mining properties and its failure to provide the same kind of incentive for the forestry interests. There are arguments both ways, but I can give the minister an example.

In the northern limits of O. and M. off the Red Lake road where there are no roads at the present time, there are great stands of overmature timber, especially balsam, which has been attacked by the spruce budworm. There are also very many overmature spruce stands north and northeast of Sioux Lookout and all the way along the C.N.R. line. Although some of the area has been leased tentatively by pulp and paper companies, at the present time no great development is taking place.
What I am coming to is this. Is there any way in which the minister's department can take the incentive in getting Ontario to put in what are properly forest roads rather than roads to resources, which seem to hinge so much upon mineral possibilities? I can give the minister an example from a copy of a letter I have that the Hornepayne chamber of commerce sent to Mr. Leslie Frost, the premier of Ontario. They asked for a road between highway 11 and highway 17 and they make this point in their letter as to what the road would do:
Access to a new mining area of incalculable potential value as it is common knowledge of prospectors here that there is a high percentage of ore-bearing rock in this area.
They go on to say:
We have a commitment from Ontario Pulp and Paper Company that, as soon as this road is open, they will commence operations on a large scale in this new territory which at present is closed to them because there is no road in or out. This would mean about 100 new families on company payroll in Hornepayne to bolster the rapidly and disastrously declining economy of this town due to the drastic layoffs and cuts in employment on the C.N.R. division of Hornepayne.
The letter goes on to say that this particular road would open up about 50,000 square miles of country unexcelled anywhere in Canada for hunting and fishing.
The three things that follow from roads in any part of the country are mineral developments, forestry developments and the hunting and fishing and tourist aspect. I know the minister knows just as well as anyone who lives there that the forestry aspect is the most important of all, not only in terms of getting at overmature stands but also because it is the basis of our whole economy. For this reason I should like to know whether there are not more imaginative steps that the minister's department can take in order to get more forest access roads into that huge part of the country.
The timber line generally follows the curve of Hudson bay but about 150 or 200 miles to the south. That means that north of Red Lake and curving around in a circle to about 120 or 125 miles north of Nakina you have a huge belt of forested country, mostly spruce,

that is still largely untapped by roads. This is the area that this major project concerns, and I wonder whether the planning of roads after an aeromagnetic survey would be as useful as planning roads on the basis of opening up the forestry potential. I should like to have the minister's opinion on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The minister is always available for any imaginative ideas. I should like to point out that in the winters of 1957-58 and 1958-59 we offered to the provinces on a 50-50 basis the building of forest access roads that would open the forests for any reason where management was assisted. I might point out that for all provinces the total amount expended was roughly $9 million and of that $9 million nearly $4 million was spent in Ontario. The next province was British Columbia with about $2J million.
I think this indicates that the province of Ontario, with its vast forested areas, took full advantage of the federal offer. However, the offer was not made available last winter on the ground that only limited use could be made of an offer to build roads from November to the end of June. In the forested areas of British Columbia particularly and also in Newfoundland and parts of Ontario nothing could be done about such roads until the snow had gone and in many areas this does not happen until near the end of May.
So that the useful part of every distance required was only about one month of construction. So the province has pressed us to see if we could not come to some agreement on a year long program of forest access roads. That is one of the matters that is now before the government. I hope the new department of forestry will take this matter in hand and see whether they cannot work out a formula with the provinces in order to achieve some of the things that we want, namely to make the maximum possible use of available manpower for winter work and still not put the province in the position of trying to get some work done during the warm summer months.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The minister knows that as a result of the switch in the pulp and paper industry there is more unemployment in winter than there used to be just as there is more employment or work in the summertime. The minister's explanation brings me to another criticism I have of both the forest access road program and the roads to resources program. I understand that in any area where crown lands are to be under long term lease to a pulp and paper company, the federal government will not make a contribution, or in other words that it has to be on crown lands free from licence. This
Supply-Northern Affairs is something like biting off your nose to spite your face. The pulp and paper companies have these huge limits, many of which they are not going to exploit for some years.
While we can be critical perhaps of the agreements that gave them these huge areas, the fact remains that roads are not going to be built there unless it is under the encouragement of an outside agency such as the provincial government or the federal government. I should like to know why it is not possible to develop a forest access road program which would go through company limits, especially in those parts of company limits where the companies do not envisage any work in the near future.
As the minister knows, the pulp and paper companies in Ontario must provide the provincial government with a 50-year plan. This marks off departments of their area and sets up a tentative long term program. This is fine in so far as that particular company developing resources on its limits in order to produce pulp is concerned, but it does not do much for the long term aspect of forest protection, forest management and access to these forests by the general public. I should like to ask the minister whether it would not be possible to see that contributions go to forest access roads that are on company limits.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: If I remember correctly we have had this discussion with the hon. member for Port Arthur in previous sessions. I made it clear then and I make it equally clear now that no limitations were imposed by the federal government on the tenure of land at all. Forest administration is purely the prerogative of the provincial government. All we offer to do is to pay 50 per cent of the cost of any of these roads under certain conditions in places the provinces want to put them, provided they are in forest areas. If you go back and look up the previous estimates when this matter was discussed you will find that I gave that information about two years ago.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, I know the minister did so, but the fact remains that the roads are not being put through the limits. Neither is this an indication that it is the province's policy to see that these roads go through crown limits that are not held by licence.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I wonder whether the minister can give me some information with regard to the expected completion date of a road in northern Manitoba. I am speaking particularly of a road leading from No. 10 highway at Simonhouse and going into the Snow lake area. I understand that approximately four contracts have been called for this road and some have been completed. On

Supply-Northern Affairs some however apparently there has not been too much work done. The people in the Snow lake area are certainly interested in knowing when this road may be completed. I should also like to have a progress report with regard to the extension of this road into the new townsite of Thompson.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The information which the hon. member is after is described here as the Osborne lake road which is from a point on the Wekusko-Snow lake road to the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company property at Osborne lake, the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company to pay one third of the cost. The mileage of this part of the road is 12. The estimated cost is $500,000 and of course the resource is mining. In addition, the work that has been done to date is the clearing of this 12.2 miles at the cost of $17,119. The only new contract of which we have information is one for the grading of this 12.2 miles for $26,767 and this is additional work to the original contract.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: To follow up that question may I say that this Osborne lake road mentioned by the minister is not the one in particular about which I was inquiring. I understand that the road from Simonhouse and going to a point near Wekusko and leading into the Snow lake area is being constructed under the roads to resources program. That is the one in which I was interested.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: This is a much bigger road than the one I described here. It is shown in our records as the Thompson road on No. 10 highway near Simonhouse and thence to a point on the Wekusko-Snow lake road to the townsite of Thompson. As to mileage, this road is 185 miles. The estimated cost is $5,200,000. Our records show that work completed on that road is clearing and grading of 50 miles at a cost of $2,566,000. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to have the opportunity to say a few words on the estimates with reference to parks, because it is the first time I have had the

opportunity since being elected to represent the constituency of Bow River to speak on these particular estimates.
I think I should say at the outset that if I do appear somewhat critical it is because the parks people are controlled and somewhat governed by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and they are unique in this regard. They are not a municipal body so that their criticisms, if they have any to express, must be expressed through their member of parliament.
I have three matters to air as grievances today, but before doing so I would like to say that the development of the parks or the development of roads in the last two or three years is such that the roads today in the national park of Banff are better than they have been for a number of years. We might start off with the main street in Banff which was criticized not only by the local people in the national park itself but by tourists. It is expected that some $310,000 will be spent to complete the main street of Banff and also the road between Jasper and Banff on which it is intended some $4,473,900 will be spent on grading between mile 68 and mile 105. Then the trans-Canada highway section is now completed through the national park at Banff and it joins with the Windermere highway, and the roads leading to Banff national park are better than they have been during the life of the park itself.
I want to discuss three matters in connection with parks, and in doing so I am making no reflection on the minister, his deputy or his officials, because I personally as member of parliament for the area have received the utmost co-operation. But because of the uniqueness of the park itself, it having no municipal council or local body except the local council which passes on their views to the department, it is necessary that some of these criticisms come through their member of parliament, and it so happens that I am the member of parliament and also a supporter of the government.
My first criticism is with reference to the expropriation of lands within the park itself. Hon. members will recall that on the orders of the day two or three days ago I asked a question with reference to this expropriation, when I mentioned there were certain parcels of land which had been expropriated from individuals who had owned land in the parks in 1955 and no settlement had yet been made. I also asked a supplementary question of the Minister of Justice and he thought that one of the cases was before the court. I might say that I have followed the matter through and I have discovered these cases as yet are not before the court.
79951-0-432
Supply-Northern Affairs
Let us look at the procedure of expropriation, and I am sure that when I am through with these remarks hon. members of the committee will appreciate why a bill of rights in some form is necessary when parks decide to expropriate land either for a purpose or without a purpose. I might say that after discussions with officials and without breaking confidence they are of opinion that they can expropriate land today for any particular purpose or just to enlarge the park area itself.
Now what is the procedure? First of all an order in council is passed and forwarded to the registrar of the proper land title office, and the order in council generally reads along these lines:
His Excellency, the Governor General in council, on recommendation of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, is pleased hereby pursuant to subsection (3) of section 6 of the National Parks Act to authorize the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to expropriate the lands described in the schedule hereto for the purpose of a national park.
Then they merely attach to that order in council the description of the land.
In all these cases there is no notice given to -the owner at all, and there is no chance of a hearing. In that regard I say that one of the most important civil rights of the people who live within the park is usurped because he has no chance, no notice and no hearing. "Well, there is a hearing if he wants one, but at his own expense, and this is the type of hearing you get. If you wish to take the matter before the exchequer court you can do so under the Expropriation Act and issue a petition of right, get before the exchequer court and have yourself heard. But by that time if the parks department are right in their interpretation of the law and the legal officers attached to the parks department and the justice department are right, they seem to be of the opinion that once the order in council is passed and placed before the registrar of the land title office, in this case in Calgary because I am dealing with the province of Alberta, and the office in Calgary is the appropriate land title office with regard to the national park, the lands themselves by that time have been expropriated and then the citizen has to sit back and wait. The land is already expropriated before such a hearing is possible.
I am sorry that I have not the names of the parties who own the parcels of land in question, but I have talked to lawyers in Calgary where their clients have consulted them with regard to their rights, and this matter has been dragging on since 1955 without settlement. In some cases the land has not been valuable, worth only about $400 or $500.

Supply-Northern Affairs
There is one case with which I will deal where the land was very valuable, worth more than $1,000,000, but the value should not enter into it. It is a civil right and if we believe in freedom of enterprise and property rights, people who own lands in fee simple in our parks should not be treated differently from people and the farmers who own land on the prairies.
There is certainly a need-and I am sure I can express myself in this regard, knowing the Prime Minister personally-for some protection, and the Prime Minister must have had some of these things in his mind when he presented his bill of rights to this parliament, because I say that the rights of people living in parks who own land which is expropriated are usurped by this type of procedure, if the procedure I have described is the law.
There should be a test case in that regard to find out if that is the procedure, because the most important point here is that once the order in council is passed then your right to own that land ceases. It seems to me that the citizen then has to go to the parks department or the Department of Justice to endeavour to get a settlement, and it drags on for five or six years before any settlement is made. That is far too long. In many cases the people need the money. In any case, under our system of jurisprudence in this country everyone should have the right to be heard when he is losing such a thing as a piece of property. He has a right to be heard and a right to be given notice.
There is another piece of land-and I cannot go into this very far because this case is before the court at this time-which concerns 60 acres of land near lake Louise. This is land a part of which was used for the trans-Canada highway. Fifty five acres or less was taken by the parks department in 1956, and when they were questioned they said that it was not taken for any particular purpose but merely to enlarge the area of the park. I suggest today that if it was right to take Mr. A's land at lake Louise-I will name the person, it was a Mr. Red Cooper, the main shareholder of a small company; I might as well mention the name-if it was right to take Mr. Cooper's land then it was right to take all the land that was owned under fee simple in the parks of this country.
I ask the minister and the officials of the department of northern affairs, to look seriously into this matter because one of the most important rights of our free enterprise system is being usurped.
There is one other ingredient which is very important: who should determine, who should decide, to take over land? I do not for a


moment suggest in this committee that there has been corruption but the danger is always present that some political party may get to know that people of another political party own certain property on crown land, and a move could then be made to expropriate that property without notice and, in many cases, without a proper settlement. I take it upon myself, as did the hon. member for Algoma, which has one of the largest parks within its borders, to bring this question to the attention of the committee, as has been done by other hon. members and by their constituents in letters and also by lawyers in the city of Calgary and lawyers in Banff and elsewhere.
Now a word on the subject of bears. Quite a bit of humour has been raised about painting bears red and so on, but I do not think our efforts up to the present time have been sufficient. I was discussing recently in Calgary the question of bears and other animals with the same propensities with a man by the name of Bill Fisher who is one of the members of the fish and game society in the province and who is known for his interest in sport throughout his years. He is a man of about 70 years of age who has hunted every type of game and fowl in Canada and who has even hunted lions in Africa, and he takes this position that when you have an animal like a bear with its propensities, it is a dangerous animal, but when nothing is being done to scare it it loses its fear of man and as a result you have these various incidents. Last year we had a girl killed in Jasper by bears. Two or three weeks ago three men were out fishing at Spray lake out of Banff. The men left their boats to unload their cars when the were attacked by the bear. These men were seriously injured. This had nothing to do with feeding. Recently a bear attacked three people on a hike in Glacier national park. I should like to read a report in the Toronto Telegram. It reads:
The Parrat boy, who lives in Clairemont, California, is recovering slowly from his injuries- a punctured lung, broken right arm and multiple gashes on his face and chest.
Alan G. Nelson, 27, a seasonal ranger-naturalist from Bismarck, N.D. has severe wounds to both thighs.
The third victim, Brita Noring, 38, of Sweden, has a mangled right foot.
From his hospital bed, ranger Nelson told of his ordeal and the youngster's pluck.
"It happened while three of us were on a fishing and hiking trip-little Smith, myself, and my roommate, Ed Mazzer, who is also a seasonal ranger naturalist.
We went about five miles and met the Swedish couple (Miss Noring and Gote Hyhlen), and about three o'clock all five us started back together.
We went about a mile when Ed Mazzer, who was in the lead, shouted 'bear, bear. Scatter!' Ed ran to the left, and the boy and I to the right. Smith and I had to run 70 yards before we found

a tree big enough to climb, and I could see the bear with two cubs over my shoulder as I ran. I looked back again and she was on top of the boy, biting, clawing and tossing him about. The bear weighed about 500 lbs and stood more than six feet tall when she reared up.
I shouted to draw her attention to me, and started climbing a tree when she made a dash for me."
For about three hours the three of them had to lie quiet and they were badly injured.
I suggest through you, Mr. Chairman, to the officials of the department that some new regulation or some new idea should be brought in to handle this situation. It does seem to me there are reliable people who go hunting and fishing. It is not a question of feeding the bears. I appreciate that, and I appreciate the regulations, and that those who do feed bears are taking a chance; they bring that trouble on themselves. But this is something different. Here the bears attack fishermen at Spray lake and attack people on a hike and last year a child was killed in Jasper.
I suggest that people who are reliable and used to hunting should be allowed to carry firearms to protect themselves. This man Bill Fisher told me he would not fish today in the parks because he would not take that chance without a gun. I say this is a serious matter and I think the whole matter should be reviewed. It is not a question of feeding the bears. It is not a question of marking them with red paint. It is a question of whether it is safe to go into the various areas in the parks where nature still exists to enjoy the fishing. I do not agree with the member from Calgary South that to thin out the bear population is sufficient.
Now, I wish to make a few observations concerning Banff itself. I was interested to note the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition in which he dealt with the amount of money spent by Canadian visitors in the United States in comparison with the amount spent by United States visitors to Canada. However, we must come to the conclusion that the tourist trade is running third as an earner of foreign exchange after wheat and newsprint. Marcus Van Steen in an article which appeared in Saturday Night on June 11, 1960 under the heading "What's Wrong with Our Tourist Industry?" reminded us:
In 1939 we had a favourable balance of $68,000,000 in the tourist exchange. By 1953 this had turned into a deficit of $63,000,000.
That deficit is continuing, and it will continue until facilities for tourists coming to Canada from the United States and other countries match those which exist in other countries. We appreciate the fact that there is only so much money that can be spent in each department, and that Rome was not 79951-0-432i
Supply-Northern Affairs built in a day, but because I am the member for Banff I must take a critical look on behalf of the people whom I represent and who have expressed criticism with regard to the facilities which exist at the present time at Banff.
Banff has been advertised by a whispering campaign as a great place at which to spend a holiday. Last year a million people came through the east gate, and that is not counting the number of people, probably half as many, who came through the west gate. The swimming pools are crowded and the other facilities are crowded, and if we are to continue to attract tourists to Canada from the United States and elsewhere it is necessary to take a serious look at the facilities, because in some cases the swimming pools we have in Banff are over-crowded to a point when in the opinion of some people the health of persons using them is endangered.
I think we should encourage freedom of enterprise, and I was interested in what the minister had to say on this subject a while ago. It is through the development of freedom of enterprise that individuals put capital into a project so that it may grow and develop. It may be that the flow of capital could be encouraged further if we took a more critical look at our economy in reference to the question of taxation.
As Governor Rockefeller said the other day, probably if our taxation was not so high today people would have more capital to invest in free enterprise industries so there would be a greater development and fuller employment in the country. As a free enterpriser I believe in that system. If we can encourage capital from private industry to go into these areas under proper supervision -and I think it has been and is available from the government-we will have a fuller and greater development than would be possible if the department were to do it itself.
I have dealt with three points today and although there are many others I could raise in summary let me say that I urge the minister from the bottom of my heart to take a serious and stern look at the question of expropriation because the rights of the people who own property in the parks are being usurped. This and similar factors may well have been in the mind of the Prime Minister in introducing his bill of rights.
I would also ask the department that it allow certain reliable people who go into the parks to fish to carry firearms for their protection, probably by licence or by permission issued through the superintendent of the park. I would also ask that the matter of facilities in the national parks be reviewed

Supply-Northern Affairs and that the government continue to encourage the third ranking industry in Canada, the tourist industry, to grow and expand.
I feel that I would be remiss in my duty if before resuming my seat I were not to express this sentiment. I know Mr. Harry Dempster, general superintendent for all western parks, Mr. Combs, superintendent of Banff national park and Mr. Cooper, superintendent of Yoho national park, all of whom are leaders in the affairs of the parks. I and all the people of Banff have always received full co-operation from them and from all the employees of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I want my acknowledgement of their courtesy and co-operation placed on the record. Any time that I or my constituents required information or assistance we have received it from these good people and other members of the department.
One final word. I wish to express the appreciation of the people of Banff to the department for assisting in the promotion of the civic centre. This has been a dream of the people there for approximately 20 years and it is now becoming a living reality. Plans have been approved by the department and it appears that within this year the civic centre will be a tangible reality and we will see the first curling rock go down the ice in Banff. This will be a source of pride and pleasure to the people of Banff and to all the tourists who visit that national park.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have had this matter under close consideration and as the hon. member knows I must work along with the historic sites and monuments board. I shall keep the hon. member informed as to developments in this connection.

While I am on my feet perhaps I could keep my promise to the hon. member for Vancouver East and answer his question about the Garibaldi park situation which has intrigued hon. members from British Columbia and others across Canada over the last several years. My records indicate that I was first required to deal with this matter when I was approached by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano and I believe one or two other hon. gentlemen from that part of British Columbia to see if I would not consider putting in a national park within two or three hours drive of Vancouver. They suggested this beautiful area called Garibaldi which is a provincial park.
On May 2, 1958 I wrote to Mr. Westwood the provincial minister and proposed that if British Columbia would turn this area over to the federal government free of encumbrances I would bring it before the federal government for consideration and if it was viewed favourably by the government we could take it over and proceed with a program of development. That letter was dated May 2, 1958 and to this date I have received no answer.
The next development was that Mr. Westwood wrote to me under date of March 9, 1960 to suggest that as a part of the centennial celebrations in 1967 the federal government and the government of British Columbia should co-operate together on a 50-50 basis to develop Garibaldi in preparation for the staging of the 1968 Olympics. In my reply I said that we would be very interested in any definite proposal that might be worked out. I mentioned in the letter that we had no policy of developing parks on a 50-50 basis with any province but that we would be interested in any definite proposal. I also said that if it were to become definite that the Olympics would be held in Garibaldi, on the basis of firm proposals and detailed plans by the province, the city and all groups interested, the question would certainly receive the most careful study. My letter was dated March 23, some four months ago.
The next item on my list of documents is the news story that emanated from Vancouver on June 24. I believe the hon. gentleman referred to this. It stated that Garibaldi was offered to the federal government and suggested that the province wanted the federal government to pay for the development of the site. This was the Squamish proposal.
Hon. members will recall that when I was asked questions in this chamber on the subject I said I had heard about the news story and would be interested in receiving a letter with some definite offer from the government of British Columbia. I also said

that if they were serious I was sure they would write and make an offer. No such offer has come forward.
The final comment I wish to make is this. The hon. member described this thing as fantastic. I think that is probably a good word to use in this connection.
