speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to speak briefly on this item but before doing so I am sure Your Honour will bear with me if I refer to the fact that we have a distinguished visitor in the gallery this afternoon, the premier of Newfoundland.
Signal Hill which is one of the most historic sites in Newfoundland and indeed in Canada was established in 1955 as a national park. Since that time the road leading to the plateau where Cabot Tower and some of the other historic sites connected with the park are located has been paved. One of the oldest buildings there, the powder magazine, has been restored. Regrettably, that is all that has been done to date. I realize, of course, that the restoration work of the tower itself could not be got under way primarily because of the fact that the tower was occupied by telecommunications people of the Department of Transport. I am advised that the telecommunications people have now vacated the tower and the tower is in effect locked up. It is rapidly falling into a state of disrepair; windows have been broken. It is regrettable that work has not commenced on the restoration of this most historic spot.
I am sure hon. members are aware that in addition to the historical significance of Signal Hill in connection with the various conflicts that took place for possession of North America between the two mother races, the English and the French, Signal Hill has also been the site of events of very great importance in the history and development of telecommunications. It is well known that at this spot in 1901 Marconi was successful in receiving his first wireless message from Cornwall, England. In addition to that, 19 years later, the Marconi people carried on successful experiments in radio telephone. The first radio telephone reception was completed on this very site in 1920. Bearing these things in mind, and bearing in mind the fact that in my opinion at any rate the department has been just a little bit lax in the restoration of historic sites in Newfoundland I should like to see work stepped up on the complete restoration of the hill area that now comprises Signal Hill park, and more particularly the restoration of the tower itself.
I can see the tower used as a museum, Mr. Chairman, but not only as a museum of historical nature in connection with the early
Supply-Northern Affairs attempts at colonization but in connection with telecommunications; for most important advances were made on this very spot. In addition to these things, the tower could also be a museum of the early days of navigation and trans-Atlantic aviation. In addition, it could be developed into a most attractive historical museum.
We are pleased to note that in connection with the new building the Newfoundland government has carried on studies into the restoration of some of the old forts of Newfoundland. During my visit to the Confederation building I was pleased to note that some of those old forts have been rebuilt to a scale model. In order for this to take place I am sure that much painstaking research had to be undertaken into the details contained in some of the vague historical references to the early fortifications in that part of Canada.
At Signal Hill park there is a custodian who has been there since 1957. As I see it there is very little need for a custodian because nothing has been done apart from the paving. I urge the minister to reply when I resume my seat and inform us what steps his department proposes to take next year toward the restoration and preservation of this site, one of the most historic sites in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As a brief answer, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I join with the hon. member for St. John's East in regretting that we were not able to do this year what we were hoping to do at Signal Hill. This is one of Canada's more historic landmarks. All I can say is that last week one of my assistant deputy ministers was down looking at Signal Hill to make further recommendations that I hope to put before the treasury board this fall to maintain this wonderful landmark in our history, and also to make the fullest possible use of it in the knowledge of what it meant so many years ago and to see that it will be maintained forever for Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would just like the committee to know that I am very serious in my remarks today, and also I am very sincere in bringing this to the attention of the committee. I quite realize there are members of the parks committee branch listening this afternoon to the proceedings of this committee, but I should like them to know that I am bringing the problems that we have at the present time in connection with our parks to the attention of the committee. In the beginning, I should like to read part of the National Parks Act:
The parks are hereby dedicated to the people of Canada for their benefit, education and enjoyment.

Supply-Northern Affairs
I should like to leave it at that for the present, Mr. Chairman, and to go on and for a few minutes this afternoon I should like to talk about our national parks and of the fact that in the constituency of Kootenay East which I represent we have a portion of three parks and I should like to offer some constructive criticism. Just recently-I should say this was a few months ago-I was approached by a member of the Shell Oil Company of Canada relative to making some scientific investigation in the Yoho park. Their letter to me reads something like this:
I would like to use the road alongside the Beaver-foot river, and camp with assistance in the area for about a week at the end of July.
This was last year:
As is well known the area is an unusual geological formation and little geological work has been done on its various problems. My aim on this occasion is to collect specimens for (1) petrographic studies on the complex (2) exhibition in the Calgary zoo- geological museum. Also to photograph and map interesting features in the area.
Every feasible or unfeasible obstacle was placed by the parks branch to discourage this request. We should encourage scientific research in all areas of Canada and especially in our national parks. We have mountains of rock in these areas and I am sure that the small samples taken from this area of unique rock formation would never be missed.
I brought a sample with me this afternoon of what was asked for in this request, and which they wished to take out of the park. This is the largest size sample that they wished to take. As I said before, there are many millions of tons of rock in the area and I am sure that this small sample which I just showed you, Mr. Chairman, if you could possibly see it from your chair, would never be missed. On my request for this concession I was informed that this could not be granted because that was the way it was handled in 1930.
Are we never going to keep up with the times, Mr. Chairman? Has the thinking of our parks branch not changed in the past 30 years? I suggest that if this is the policy, which I find it hard to believe, now is the time to revise our present regulations. After all, Mr. Chairman, it was a part of our election promises that "now is the time for a change". After 25 years under the previous administration I think that now is the time for a change in these regulations. I should like to read another part of the reply of the department which I received to this request.
Since I wrote you on October 2, 1959, enclosing a permit authorizing the collection of specimens and the use of the fire road to the Ice river area, the broad question of permitting in future the collection of botanical, mineral, fossil and other specimens from the national parks has been under review.


The removal of these small items of rock from our national parks has to go through the head office of the parks branch. The letter continues:
As a matter of fact, the officers of the branch who have undertaken this study have not yet completed their research-
Can you imagine, Mr. Chairman? There has to be research with respect to the removal of small pieces of rock for the Calgary museum, which is also a public institution.
-and, consequently, I am most reluctant to issue further permits at this time. I am sure you realize that the removal from the national parks of any form of specimens is actually a breach of the dedication clause of the National Parks Act which provides that the parks shall be maintained and made use of so as to leave them unimpaired for future generations. While it may be argued that the impairment in this case is very small, nevertheless it is a fact that applications for permits of various kinds have increased greatly over the past few years.
It is hoped to have the matter reviewed and a decision reached before the coming spring-[DOT]
About seven months later.
-is well advanced and I will be only too glad to inform you of the decision which has been reached at that time. In the meantime, I am sure you will appreciate why it is not possible for me to grant the necessary permission immediately.
The parks were set aside for the benefit, education and enjoyment of the people of Canada. I read that from the act, but so far I cannot see that we are getting a great deal of enjoyment out of them. After all when we buy a new suit I do not think we are inclined to take the new suit, hang it in a cellophane bag, put it away in a closet and save it for our grandchildren. Nor do we build ourselves a new home and say that we are going to have it for the generation that is going to follow some time after the year 2060 which would be 100 years from now.
What we are missing is the fact that we want to get pleasure out of these parks today. The regulations of the National Parks Act passed in 1930 are so out of date and outmoded that now is the time that the act should be amended to bring it into line with present day conditions. Our parks today, due to their location, are hampering industry and the expansion of the rest of the province. I refer specifically to the province of British Columbia. In several instances our lumbering industry has been forced to make long detours around our parks because of the fact that no provision for trucking through the park areas has been made and, further, it is apparent that the parks branch is making no effort to adjust this situation.
While I am talking about the park areas I should like to point out to the committee that it has been brought home very forcibly to me by the parks branch that park areas

will not be developed until such time as they are turned over to the department tor further work. I believe consideration should be given with respect to leases on motels and hotels situated on park land. Here are a few of the troubles now plaguing their owners in our parks. I should like to refer to a matter which was determined by the courts in the province of British Columbia in the year 1958 and I should like to include in Hansard part of the findings and also part of the brief submitted at that time. The brief reads in part as follows:
In the spring of 1958 I was consulted by five hotel and motel owners whose properties were situate in Kootenay national park in the vicinity of Radium Hot Springs. They had been assessed by the provincial taxation department on the land on which the motels and hotels were situate and were also assessed on the improvements, i.e., the buildings which they had built or furnished. These owners held leases or licences from the parks commission or, in other words, from the dominion government, which were renewable more or less indefinitely although the parks commission had the right to refuse renewal at any termination if it so desired. There was also a provision stating that in the event of cancellation all buildings had to be removed or demolished within a given period. You can easily see that it would be impossible to move even a small house through the canyon-
The reference is to Sinclair canyon.

and neither of the hotels could be moved in any event, so that this provision simply meant that the lessee would lose all the improvements which he had built or purchased on the terms of the lease or licence.
At this time all five of the hotel and motel owners were advised that the provincial government under the provincial taxation act had a perfect right to tax them for the occupancy of the crown land but had no right to tax them on improvements, and in consequence they were instructed to appeal the assessments. All five assessments were appealed to the court of revision and the court upheld the hotel and motel owners, stating that the improvements were not taxable. Here is what happened to these people in a national park. The brief continues:
The provincial government appealed and the case came before the board of revision. The board came from Victoria to Cranbrook and heard all five appeals and again upheld the decision of the court of revision that the improvements were not taxable. This year (1959) the five owners who had appealed successfully last year received assessment notices taxing the land only but other owners inside the park who had not appealed got notices taxing both land and improvements although the court of revision had already held last year that such improvements were not taxable.
Four owners who had been assessed on both land and improvements instructed the lawyer to appeal to the court of revision to be held at Golden in the spring of 1959. The matter was appealed and again the court
Supply-Northern Affairs of revision held that the improvements were not taxable, but the government assessor who was present then produced a copy of a bill- this is hard to believe-which was at that time before the provincial house, amending the taxation act so that the improvements were taxable and making this amendment retroactive to 1957.
That is what has happened in the case of motels and hotels constructed in one of our national parks for the benefit of the touring public. They are being taxed out of business. The brief continues:
The retroactive feature had the effects of nullifying the decision of the court of revision and the board of revision held in 1958, and instead of gaining anything by last year's appeals the clients are out their costs of both appeals and have to pay taxes on the improvements for 1958 which had been held to be invalid. In other words, they were fined the costs of their appeal for daring to appeal against the provincial government.
It is pointed out that the retroactive feature of this tax smells to the high heavens and that if the practice continues no one knows where it will end and what effect it will have on the improving of accommodation in our national parks. I could go on to refer to a considerable number of other items at this time but I should like to bring to the attention of the committee some of the problems that the motel and hotel owners in our national parks are having. The motel owners are only allowed to be open for business during the summer months. They are prohibited from remaining open in the winter months. Only a caretaker is permitted to remain on the premises. Yet at the same time owners just outside the park area are in many cases able to rent their cabins all winter to old age pensioners or people in reduced circumstances.
The owners not only have to pay full taxation to the provincial government on both land and improvements, to which matter I have just referred, but they also have to pay their licence fees to the federal government. The park owners of hotels and motels have to pay a business licence fee to the federal government and in addition have to pay separate federal licence fees for the following, tobacco counter, souvenir counter and dining room licence.
With regard to licensed premises in the park, the licensee has to pay to the provincial liquor control board 2 per cent on draft beer with an annual minimum of $75, no tax on bottled beer, and a minimum licence of $150 a year on spirits and wines, and in addition has to pay to the federal government 2 per cent on draft beer, 2 per cent on bottled beer and 4 per cent on wines and spirits, while the outside owners holding

Supply-Northern Affairs licences only have to pay the provincial liquor licences. The park owners also have to pay in addition to their annual licence or rental charges, water charges, sewage charges and garbage charges that have been assessed to them while in the parks property.
There is one other item on this particular problem that I should like to bring to your attention. It is certainly a very heavy charge on the hotel and motel owners in the area and I am sure that many of them would like it considered.
In reviewing the northern affairs report I have come across some very interesting figures. I find that in the national parks branch we have a revenue of $2,190,890 and expenditures of $22,095,425. The visitors to the national parks of Canada totalled 3,940,711 in 1957-58. The cost to the taxpayers of Canada was approximately $7 for every visitor that entered our parks. Let us face the issue. It is not the cost of the whole northern affairs branch; it is the cost of the national parks branch. That is just an item about which I am greatly interested.
The taxpayers of Canada are subsidizing all these affairs and at the same time we are not getting value back, even though as my hon. friend said there were some millions of dollars spent in Canada, but I do not think you can attribute that to the deficit in our parks area. Another item is that of camp sites. We spent $1,123,436 in addition on camp ground sites. Three parks in my area, Glacier national park, Yoho national park and Kootenay national park are so situated along the border of Alberta and British Columbia that it has hampered industry, especially in my area. We have a great development there in mining and lumber. In order to reach the prairie markets on the eastern side of the Rockies we either have to travel 100 miles north or 100 miles south, both coming and going, in order to get our products into the markets of the prairies.
As I mentioned in my talk a few moments ago, we in Kootenay East are dependent on industry for the economy of the area. I think that some provision should be made, if the parks branch are not going to allow trucks which are accepted on all of the main highways of the country, for another road to be constructed. We have only three passes in that area by means of which we can get into the prairie markets.
As to access roads to parks, this has been a problem over a great number of years. I feel that going back 20 years our access roads have been important to our parks. I believe we should develop them. We want our own people to go into our parks that is what we want now. We want them to go there and
[Mr. McFarlane.l

we want them to enjoy themselves. But in many cases our access roads have not reached the state where they are attracting the tourist population into the country. Back in 1936 Hon. H. H. Stevens spoke to this House of Commons and pleaded with the government of the day to build access roads into the parks, namely Glacier national park, Yoho national park and Kootenay national park and he was successful to a certain extent. But in the last 25 years the travelling public are demanding more and more. They are demanding good accommodation and good roads. They are travelling in trailers and cars and they are doing so at greater speeds, I think we should consider these access roads not only in the province of Alberta but in the province of British Columbia.
The three park areas that I have mentioned cover approximately 1,571 square miles. It is a great deal of territory. If we are going to develop it I think the people should be allowed to come into all the areas of these parks and visit them without a great deal of red tape. If a man wants to go in or a tourist wishes to go into the park he should be able to contact the superintendent or the assistant superintendent and receive permission to go into the park without having to be obliged to go through all the departments of government because many of them get so fed up that by the time the application is accepted they do not want to go in anyway.
As far as I can see, unless we are going to develop these parks, what we need is a highway through the parks and about 100 yards on each side. I believe if I went around and asked each one who had been there if he had left the main highway in any one of our national parks I think without exception I would find that not one had left the main highway to our parks. That is what is happening to all of this 1,571 square miles we have put into our park areas.
I was also quite interested in a brief which I saw just a short time ago in the U.S. National Parks Magazine entitled "A National Policy". I was quite interested in item No. 2 on page 2 which reads as follows:
National parks and national nature monuments are set aside for the enjoyment,-
That is my request at the moment.
-scientific study and permanent preservation, in a natural state, of the native plant and animal life-
And so on. I quite agree with that. But at the same time I believe we could make our parks so that people are going to get enjoyment out of them today, not tomorrow or next year. I believe that in the economic changes that are coming into our country and the expansion that we are going to have we

are not too sure that the people of Canada want all this preservation and all this parks preservation in their natural state.
I was quite pleased with the remarks of some of the members about bears. I could not possibly let this opportunity go by without a certain comment about the matter. I was pleased to receive a circular about bears put out by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. There is just one thing I find wrong with it. It is not printed on red paper. It is quite consistent with the health of animals and that type of approach. There is also an item here that says a deodorizer is very effective. If I see a bear of any kind I am not going to look for a deodorizer.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Nor is anybody else.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
In closing may I say this.
I cannot help bringing to the minister's attention the matter of the Olympic games. We in British Columbia are all interested in the Olympic games situation. At the present time we have a situation wherein first I think we want the winter Olympic games to be in Canada. I think we should process it along that way first, that we want them absolutely in Canada. British Columbia and part of Alberta are the only places in which it would be suitable to hold the winter Olympic games in view of the fact that we have the Rocky mountains at our back door. Several places have been suggested, but what have been suggested are certain undeveloped areas. In view of the many millions of dollars that have been spent on our national parks I believe it would be excellent if we could take the Olympic games out of the national parks. I think they should be placed in an undeveloped area so that we are going to spread our development all over British Columbia because I feel that it is to British Columbia that they are going to come. I should also like to ask the minister's consideration of Cedar valley near the city of Fernie. In this particular place you have winter and summer all at the same time. You have skiing on the upper slopes and also have plenty of room for any other development that you wish to put in. I believe that is all I have to say at this time, Mr. Chairman. I hope the minister will reply to some of my questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I
hope that the minister will take some satisfaction in knowing that there has been considerable gratification in Okanagan-Revel-stoke riding over the substantial increase in the monetary allotment for the development of both Mount Revelstoke and Glacier parks in the last two years and for accelerating the pace of development. I should explain I
Supply-Northern Affairs think that the hon. member for Kootenay East and I share Glacier national park and both of us have a common problem that when people hear Glacier national park mentioned they think of the one in the United States, whereas there is a very fine park by the same name somewhat older between Golden and Revelstoke which is about to become more readily available to the public now than was the case when it was first created.
It is because of this situation that I trespass on the time of the committee to make reference to the development program of these two parks. When the Minister of Public Works was dealing with his estimates earlier this week he referred to the fact that the trans-Canada highway through Mount Revelstoke national park should be completed by the end of the present construction season and that the trans-Canada highway link through Glacier national park should be or could be completed by the end of next year's construction season. This will mean to both parks, but to Glacier park in particular which has not until now been accessible by highway, a tremendous influx of travel, both of Canadian and foreign tourists.
Glacier park is and has been almost from its beginning a wilderness with very limited facilities for the accommodation of visitors. Since the dismantling of Glacier house at Glacier station there have been no facilities in any way in keeping with the standards of the tourist accommodation to be expected as a matter of course today. As the minister knows, at the camp site in Glacier there are two pipes for water, a couple of kitchen shelters and some rather unsophisticated sanitary arrangements. I think in view of this fact and that within one or two years there will be a tremendous flood of tourist traffic over the newly completed trans-Canada highway, it is essential that all development be directed toward coinciding the completion of at least the beginning of modern facilities with the opening of the highway.
I realize it is not possible to do everything which has been visualized at once and I also realize that the splendid attractions in the park very much depend on planning and development. The increase in votes of money allotted to these two parks in the last two years is evidence that this requirement is governing the thinking of the parks planners and the branch. But I wonder if even now the park is going ahead rapidly enough. Time is running out. It is a short construction season in the mountains and there is much to be done. I hope the minister can make a report to the committee on how progress is developing, particularly in Glacier but also in Mount Revelstoke park.
6856	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs
So far as Mount Revelstoke is concerned, the largest item of concern there, as the minister knows, is the road to the summit of the park. The summit is the justification for Mount Revelstoke park. The trails, the lakes, the opportunities for hiking and the wildlife are in those highland plateaux on the summit of Mount Revelstoke. The road there now was built 40 to 50 years ago. So far as the width is concerned it has not been improved to a very great extent. The surface certainly is good. It is a safe road but a narrow one. It is 18 miles to the summit. Already restrictions are placed on cars pulling trailers; in fact, trailers are not permitted to go to the summit.
I realize that last year a study was made of the possibility of a second road, a down road on the southeastern slopes of the mountain, to take some of the pressure off the mountain road to the summit. Apparently that has been abandoned and now a survey is going on this year on the possibility of reconstructing the present road. I would emphasize to the minister that in view of the nature of the terrain and the difficulties of construction of the road, unless the greatest acceleration is given to this survey and to the commencement of reconstruction of that road, the work will coincide with the arrival of the very greatly increased flow of tourist traffic along the trans-Canada highway, part of which passes through the boundaries of Mount Revelstoke park. I would suspect that a very large number of travellers coming through will want to drive to the summit of Mount Revelstoke, and it would be very regrettable if the construction work on that road coincided with this great influx of new travel.
I also feel I should extend the appreciation of the city of Revelstoke to the department for the close attention which has been given to the development of the ski slopes; the Nels Nelson jump hill, the slalom hill and so on. I hope that the plans undertaken there are also taking into account the possibility of opening the summit of the mountain to skiing during the winter months. There is approximately 10 feet of powdered snow there during the winter and a six-month season, and I understand it would take as little as $15,000 to keep the road to the top open and make that facility accessible.
I would like to draw the minister's attention to the fact that the citizens of the city of Revelstoke are most anxious to cooperate in any way with the parks branch in making the facilities of Mount Revelstoke more attractive to visitors. The city of Revelstoke is in a rather unique position in relation to the park in that almost the 

whole of the eastern boundary of Revelstoke borders on the park. It is not like Banff or Jasper, which are located in the park itself, but the park looms large in the life of the community. The citizens there have a great desire to co-operate with the branch. I know they are sincere and I hope a means can be found to provide very close liaison between the citizens and the parks branch.
Lastly, I think it would be only fitting to pay tribute to the work of a very dedicated and admired man in Revelstoke, the superintendent of the two parks, Mr. B. R. Styles, whose work and public relations are most highly esteemed in the community and who is doing a magnificent piece of work on behalf of the branch.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, so far I have been able to resist the temptation to intervene in the controversy as to what particular locality in the far west should be the site of the winter Olympic games in 1968. But I would point out to the minister that unless a decision is made on this point pretty soon there will be no possibility of holding the winter Olympic games in Canada at all.
The hon. member for Kootenay East said that the first thing to do was to decide whether the games would be held in Canada at all and to get a decision on that from the international Olympics committee, then we could decide in what part of Canada the games should be held. With respect, that is the wrong way to proceed, because the international Olympics committee will not choose any particular country as the site of either the winter Olympics or the summer Olympics unless that country goes to the committee with a plan drafted and prepared in detail, and that applies particularly to the winter Olympics.
Therefore the first thing is to decide where we will have the games in Canada. Then we should prepare a detailed plan, include all the facilities which would be available, and satisfy the committee that we can hold the games in Canada. Not until that is done is there any possibility of getting a decision as to whether they will be held in Canada at all.
Therefore, it is a matter of immediate urgency from the point of view of the department concerned making a decision, which will not be an easy one as far as one can gather from this discussion, as to what part of Canada is most suitable for the holding of these games in case the international committee decides Canada will be the country. I leave that on the minister's doorstep.
I understand that the provincial government of Ontario has decided to establish a provincial park in the Elliot Lake area

and I would ask whether any request for cooperation has been received from the federal department. I hope that if such a request is made everything will be done to help bring this about at the earliest date.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Perhaps I may deal with the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition first. I should like to start with the last point he raised with regard to a provincial park at Elliot Lake. I have kept in contact with the uranium committee on these plans, along with the hon. member for Essex West who is one of the strong boosters for getting a provincial park at Elliot Lake. So far there has been no official request to our department for help. We would be willing to give it if we were asked, but I should like to point out that Ontario has one of the finest parks departments in all Canada. Last year they had 50 parks, and now they have 60; they are adding about 10 a year, and they realize this is of great importance to the people of Ontario. They are very skilled. There have even been suggestions that the smaller parks such as Georgian bay and the St. Lawrence parks should be turned over to the provincial governments who could do a better job in regard to them than we could. As I say, we are willing to help, though we are not expecting that we shall be asked to do so.
This gives me an opportunity to clear away this ghost from my attic-this matter of the Olympic games. In the first place, I have nothing to do with the Olympic games. If that comes under any department of government, it comes under the Department of National Health and Welfare. It does seem unfair that I have had to carry the burden in this respect because one of the groups desiring to have the games in this area was seeking the use of a national park and, second, because another group putting forward the claims of a particular area for the games were hoping to have the site made into a national or provincial park so that somebody would take over the responsibility for providing the facilities.
I think the Leader of the Opposition is wrong on another point. The Olympic games committee says it is their decision which place Canada should recommend, but once the Olympic committee makes that decision there has to be an agreement between them and a body known as the F.I.S. which has to set the standards and then there has to be an agreement between the provinces, the federal government and the municipality as to how much money they can put up. There have been meetings about this, because most
Supply-Northern Affairs Canadians are interested in seeing that Canada should take its proper part in this great event, but I should like to disclaim any responsibility for making this decision as to where the games are held in Canada. Second, my responsibility as minister in charge of parks only comes in if they happen to be held in an area over which I have jurisdiction.
Several hon. members, including the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke, the hon. member for Kootenay East and the hon. member for Bow River dealt with the question of national parks. This gives me an opportunity to say something in this committee that I have said outside the house, something which I said off the cuff some months ago. It is my feeling, as minister in charge of parks, that it is about time all those millions of people in Canada who use the parks and love them should band together and form themselves into a national parks association. This should not be an association composed of civil servants or politicians; it should be an association of people who use the parks and are friends of the parks. They should have an information service which would spread all through their membership, and far beyond it, explaining what the purposes of the parks are. How can a minister stand up against the pressures of commercial interests who want to use the parks for mining, forestry, for every kind of honky-tonk recreational device known to man, unless the people who love these parks are prepared to band together and support the minister by getting the facts out across the country?
As I listened to this discussion this afternoon I could not help but feel the necessity of a national parks association doing educational work among the members of the house. Hon. members should be aware of the fundamental purpose of the parks, which is to preserve, as they were in the beginning, those beautiful scenic areas of our country in order that our children and our children's children for generations to come may go there and find certain areas where the country is the same as its original discoverers found it. That is the primary purpose of the national parks.
At the same time there is a second function of those responsible for the administration of these parks, and that is how to make these beautiful places as accessible to the Canadian pepole as possible. There is a clash between these two purposes. The parks department has had to stand up in favour of these basic purposes against those forces which would like to exploit the parks and use up all their resources quickly in their lifetime and leave nothing for the generations
6858	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs that will follow. I, as minister, want to make it abundantly clear that I stand for the primary purpose of these parks. At the same time I will do everything possible to make these beautiful parks available to the people of Canada if they have a full conception of what they are there for.
Let me inform the committee of another salient fact. No one could have more knowledge than myself about the real value of these parks and their place in the national life, because I have spent during many summers periods of six or eight weeks at a time in these places, not living up in one of those ritzy cottages that are reserved for specially favoured visitors. I have camped out in the little camp sites. I have lived in tents. I have stayed in the shack tents and I have visited occasionally in the portable cabins used by better-off visitors. My sympathies are With the man who has not too much money; my sympathies are with the thousands who want these parks and who want them for their quietness and beauty and relief from the pressures of this civilization; the people who do not go there for the purpose of doing something which they could do just as well in any place outside. If people want to shoot off bullets at a rifle range, or take out electric cars thumping around a circular iron track, or attend open air theatre shows, then I say there are many areas outside the parks which could perfectly well provide such diversion.
I hope we can make friendly arrangements with the provinces with regard to this. I know that hon. members who represent park constituencies are constantly under pressure from the people of the area to try to get certain changes made in park operations, but I should like those members to be allies of mine-men who stand at my right and left, as minister, to tell the people boldly and clearly what these parks are for-so they will be given what they want, if possible, provided it is in harmony with the purposes of the parks. If hon. members do that, I think they will find that 90 per cent of the people in their areas will be behind them.
It is only the 5 per cent or the 10 per cent who put on these pressures and who seem to bother hon. members because they can write letters to the press and get editorials published in newspapers. The rest of the people, the great majority, heartily approve the purposes for which these parks are now kept, and these are the people who should be standing up and supporting these objectives when we discuss this matter of their administration. I want to make my position clear, without misunderstanding as to where I stand on this issue.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as one who has not a national park in his constituency I feel safely out of this part of the discussion. I listened attentively to the minister's explanation about Garibaldi and the boondoggling tactics that provincial government officials in British Columbia have been carrying on and in the light of this I should like to offer a solution to the problem. I think the minister and his department recognize the need for a national park in the populous central Pacific coast. I should like to recommend an area on Vancouver island which has been well known for many years as a splendid recreational area for skiing, summer camping and other activities. It is a beautiful alpine area known as the forbidden plateau.
Most of the area belongs to the Canadian Pacific railway or the E. & N. and was acquired as part of a land grant. It is not commercially timbered. I think the minister might be able to make a very favourable arrangement with the C.P.R. for a few square miles of this area which would be sufficient for the purpose. It is very easy of access and it would cost very little to extend road services into it. It would not remove resources from development in the area.
I just throw this out as a suggestion because apparently we are not going to get anywhere with the Garibaldi park issue and I do not think the people of British Columbia should have to be denied the pleasure of having a national park because of certain provincial politics. The area is within a few hours of Vancouver-as a matter of fact possibly three and a half to four hours-and within about three hours of Victoria and within a few more hours of Seattle and Tacoma. I think it comes very close to fulfilling all the requirements of a park in that area.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I intend to erupt on a later item but as a socialist I cannot resist rising and expressing my complete support for the minister's explanation of his philosophy in connection with the development of national parks. It is the right philosophy and is well received by this group. Those who want to go to night clubs and circuses can find them in larger cities. I am all for the preservation of natural beauty and features in our parks and their development along the lines suggested by the minister.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to delay passage of the minister's estimates. I have just one point I should like him to consider. This year marks the 350th anniversary of the founding of Cupids by John Guy. I suggest that the minister

give consideration to the marking of the site where John Guy erected the standard of King James I in 1610.

speechtext: In view of the support the minister received from the hon. member for Kootenay West I have a suggestion to make. The hon. gentleman is in favour of the preservation of wilderness areas for ordinary people. I have a feeling that if he were approached in the proper spirit by the minister he might be open to persuasion to co-operate in creating a situation through which a national park could come into being in this magnificent area, perhaps called Her-ridge national park.

speechtext:
During the last two years I have received approximately six letters from Mr. Douglas H. Mahon in Halifax. Such industry deserves attention and I feel obliged to place this man's argument before the minister. In a recent letter he states:
Supply-Northern Affairs
Just today I read a special dispatch to the Telegram ol Toronto describing a speech the Hon. Alvin Hamilton is reported to have made in Port Arthur in that a switch in federal policy toward parks and recreation areas will be announced soon following a national conference on conservation in Ottawa next month. A goal of a billion dollars' worth of travel business In Canada in 1960 through the co-operation of provincial municipal Mr. Hamilton is reported to have said.
This quotation is interesting: "The federal government can no longer indulge only in provision of recreation for the leisured classes but rather it must provide recreation for the leisured masses as well."
This man is a skiing enthusiast and has asked me to ask the minister on his estimates to give consideration to developing ski trails and promoting skiing in the parks in the maritime regions. He suggests that this would be a valuable assistance to the park in Nova Scotia.
I have another point. When one enters a national park one is aware through signs that it is a project of the federal government. Has the minister considered putting signs or symbols on all projects to which the federal government contributes. Many ordinary people who do not take an interest in government wonder what the federal government does. Of course it is involved in the trans-Canada highway and various road programs yet there is no symbolic evidence of any permanent kind to make the public aware of what it does.
In most of the states south of the border there are signs indicating that the federal government has made a contribution to various projects. Could the minister not work out a symbol that would be recognized as a federal standard indicating that the federal government has contributed to the project? These could be liberally distributed. I do not suggest he go as far as some provincial cabinet ministers and have his own name splattered all over the place because one assumes he may move on to another portfolio or that the government may change. There should be a symbol such as the maple leaf or beaver or something to indicate that the federal government has contributed to the project. This would help make known to the ordinary people the role the federal government plays in many fields where recognition is not now accorded to it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
276. Canadian wildlife service-wildlife resources conservation and development, including administration of the Migratory Birds Convention Act, $714,680.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few remarks on this item. First of all, I am pleased to see that there is an increase of close to $28,000 in this vote. I have always been keenly interested in Canadian wildlife and in this branch because it is one branch of government that has a certain reverence for life. This branch has made a valuable contribution toward the preservation of wildlife, in co-operation with the provincial governments and various sportsmen's and other organizations and also the administration of the Migratory Birds Convention Act. As a matter of fact, in my opinion the service is a defence against the very often apparent thoughtless power-hungry dam builders who


very often are not concerned with the effects of their activities on human beings or wildlife.
I happen to represent a constituency that is very interested in both of these questions. In our district we have an organization that takes a very active part in giving consideration to the preservation of wildlife, game and fish, and also to the effect of possible hydro development on the wildlife of the district, namely the west Kootenay rod and gun club association, which has a considerable membership in our district because hunting and fishing are enjoyed by a large number of people. Both hunting and fishing are excellent in the Kootenay area, as a matter of fact, the best in Canada. Because of that they want to preserve this good hunting and fishing.
At a recent meeting held by the association they gave consideration to the possible developments in the Columbia basin and adopted a resolution which I intend to read. I might say before doing so that this resolution is endorsed by the British Columbia rod and gun clubs association and by a number of other associations interested in the conservation and development of our wildlife resources. They have asked me to bring this to the attention of the committee on this estimate and to urge the consideration of their proposal. The resolution reads as follows:
Whereas the impact on wildlife of Kootenay river and Columbia river development of power and storage dams will be tremendous and the adequate correction of the problems created will be much beyond the financial ability of the fish and game branch of the department of recreation and conservation of the government of British Columbia.
Therefore be it resolved (1) that a complete and detailed biological survey be carried out jointly by the Canadian wildlife service and the fish and game branch, British Columbia department of recreation and conservation to determine the ecological effect on wildlife of each and all proposed power and storage dams, the report of such survey to be publicly available.
(2)	That anticipated problems in wildlife management as indicated in the survey be planned for. rectified, and financed as part of said developments.
(3)	That a definite proportion of the value of the power produced be set aside and other benefits such as navigation, irrigation, etc. (including downstream benefits) produced from said developments for wildlife management and recreational facilities in the Kootenay and Columbia river basins in Canada.
I have read the resolution at the request of the west Kootenay rod and gun club association and the British Columbia association of rod and gun clubs. I do urge the minister to give serious consideration to these proposals which are the result of a study made by a committee as to the likely effect of these developments on the wildlife in the area.

Before concluding, may I say I have been asked particularly to express the appreciation of the west Kootenay rod and gun club association for the services rendered to our district by the officials of this branch which I think should be known not as the wildlife service but as the reverence for wildlife service, a bit of a contrast to some other organizations. There are always people who are interested in conserving wildlife and natural resources. They are a little different in background and outlook from some of the brash representatives of modern industry. However, they do appreciate the good work being done in the district, and particularly the advice, investigation and co-operation they have received in respect of the preservation of that life known as the wildlife at Duck lake. That is all I wish to say at this time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a question for the minister on this item. As indicated by its name, Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, my constituency has in the centre of it a very fine body of water, Last Mountain lake, which is over 50 miles in length. This lake is a great summer attraction for boating and fishing. It is also a favourite spot for geese and ducks in the fall. It is a real sportsman's paradise. Unfortunately, however, much of the farm and pasture land around the lake, particularly near the towns of Nokomis, Govan, Simpson and Imperial, is also a favourite resting and feeding place for some other large birds that are not so welcome. I refer to the sandhill crane.
Under this item, 276, concerning administration of the Migratory Birds Convention Act, I should like to mention a problem I have had brought to my attention many times by farmers in the area mentioned. It concerns the damage to crops and pastures by these sandhill cranes during their flight southward each fall. Great loss is caused by these large and hungry birds, both in what they eat and by the dirt they leave in pastures where much of the grass is made unfit for grazing. I believe that sandhill cranes are protected by federal laws under the Migratory Birds Convention Act. I realize that this protection is a safeguard for the preservation of the nearly extinct whooping crane, which to a certain extent resembles the sandhill crane. With regard to this necessary protection for whooping cranes and also in consideration of the damage done by the sandhill cranes I have here a resolution passed unanimously at the last annual meeting of the rural municipality of Wreford, No. 280, in Nokomis. Part of the resolution reads as follows:
Whereas sandhill cranes are protected by the federal government, be it resolved that the federal
Supply-Northern Affairs
government take immediate steps to protect and compensate farmers for the losses of grain crops as well as pastures.
I wonder whether the minister would comment on this problem in the Last Mountain lake area. I understand there is some suggestion of an automatic exploder system to frighten the birds from the crops. I also believe that payment for crop damage is probably a provincial responsibility. With regard to compensation for loss, can the minister state, although I know it does not come under his department, whether such loss would be recovered by crop insurance if the Saskatchewan C.C.F. government sees fit to accept the federal government's offer to help pay for such a crop insurance plan in Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I cannot answer the last part of the hon. member's question. As to the first part, may I say to him that I am quite aware of the serious problem that exists along the flyway of the sandhill cranes. They are increasing rapidly in numbers and the great harm they do to pastures and to the areas along their flyway is well known. The wildlife service is faced with a very serious difficulty in that the flyway of the sandhill crane overlaps in part the flyway of the whooping crane, which we are trying very hard to preserve. I think there are just 39 of them left.
The Saskatchewan government, on behalf of the people of Saskatchewan, has been negotiating with the federal government as to what we can do to help. It is quite true that this fall, an experiment is going to be tried of using exploding devices, aircraft and so on, to see if we cannot move the birds along the flyway a little faster in order to get them out of the grain areas where farmers are suffering serious losses. If we are forced into giving permission to shoot sandhill cranes we run the danger that because of their similarity to the whooping crane one or two whoopers may be knocked off. The matter is being given very active consideration and serious efforts are being made to see if we cannot get around the difficulty caused by the sandhill cranes on the one hand and at the same time preserve the whooping crane.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Has the minister any relative statistics over the last few years with respect to whooping cranes? He mentioned a figure of 39. How does that compare with five years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am informed that in the mid-forties the figure was down to 15. Five years ago it had climbed to 22 and now it is up to 39.

Supply-Northern Affairs

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Will the minister tell us how these explosive devices will differentiate between sandhill cranes and whooping cranes? It seems to me that we can afford to lose a little excess grain in order to preserve our wildlife. As a city dweller I am quite sure that my people would not like to see anything done by the department which would have any effect upon wildlife, particularly such species as whooping cranes, which were almost extinct.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The exploding device does not kill. All it does is to frighten the birds, and I do not think there is any serious harm to the birds that are frightened.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister will remember that under this vote there was a board set up in his department in connection with water levels. This board had to do with the handling of water levels and the regulation of the discharge of water from lake Ontario and the flow of water in the international rapids section. The board, in conjunction with the international joint commission and also after consultation with the United States members, I believe, recommended and approved a method of regulation concerning the flow of water out of lake Ontario and the discharge of water into the international rapids section.
Arising out of that method of regulation, which has been amended from time to time, there is a dispute between the power entities and the governments of Canada and the United States as to the responsibility for damages which may result from the inauguration of the method of control. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
279. Studies and surveys of the Columbia river watershed in Canada, $98,745.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I rise to say a few words on this item which provides $98,745 for studies and surveys on the Columbia river watershed in Canada. 1 note that the item has been reduced by nearly $72,000 since last year. I therefore assume that the expenditures on these surveys are drawing to a close. I have a few remarks to make and I want to ask the minister a few questions as to who is responsible for these surveys, and who will be doing the work and where during the coming season.
In rising to speak on these estimates I am representing the views of many people in my constituency and elsewhere in British Columbia who are concerned about the proposals put forward by Premier Bennett of British Columbia to build a dam known as the high Arrow on the Arrow lakes. I might say that I am supported by large numbers of persons who are either members or supporters of all political parties. As a matter of fact, it is a bit cheering for a socialist to get a letter from a delightful lady who is a supporter of the Conservative party and in which she says this: We can depend on you because we know you have never been the pawn of any corporation or company; or from a Liberal who says: We are pleased that you are giving a lead in this matter and have stated clearly where you stand; or from a Social Crediter who says that while he supports the government of British Columbia in most respects, he cannot support Premier Bennett's proposal for the building of a high Arrow dam. Therefore, with every assurance that I represent a large number of people in my constituency and in other places in the interior and in British Columbia I can say that we who oppose high Arrow are united with one purpose
G864	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs in mind, namely to preserve the Arrow lakes and to support a development of the Columbia river that will not bring unnecessary destruction of our natural resources. In spirit, regardless of party, we all belong to the Columbia conservation fraternity.
In that connection, in order to indicate to some of the hon. members who do not realize the ghastly tragedy that might happen if some people have their way, I want to quote briefly from a book on the Columbia river written by Professor Lyman. He is writing about the Columbia river between Revelstoke and the Arrow lakes down as far as Robson and he states as follows:
The journey down the Arrow lakes from Arrowhead to Robson Is one to dream of, one to recall in waking hours, and even, we almost suspect, in another life. The two lakes together constitute 130 miles of steamboating, and every mile has its special charm.
In dealing with the type of mind that produces or supports this type of proposal, before going on to my more definite statement, I wish to quote from a book entitled "More in Anger" by Marya Mannes. She writes some interesting articles at times. At page 41 of her book she says this:
Who is so rich as that? Slowly the wasters and despoilers are impoverishing our land, our nature, and our beauty, so that there will not be one beach, one hill, one lane, one meadow, one forest free from the debris of man and the stigma of his improvidence.
Who is so rich that he can squander forever the wealth of earth and water for the trivial needs of vanity or the compulsive demands of greed; or so prosperous in land that he can sacrifice nature for unnatural desires? The earth we abuse and the living things we kill will, in the end, take their revenge; for in exploiting their presence we are diminishing our future.
I think that puts the case very well against those who support hydro developments which bring about the unnecessary destruction of natural resources.
1 should now like to give hon. members a little history on this question because I have been very close to it for many years. Certain interests in the United States who apparently mesmerized some of our British Columbia officials some years ago have been urging the building of the high Arrow dam since 1945, particularly former Senator Dill in the first instance, Senator Magnasser in the second instance, and other senators. In this connection I wish to quote very briefly from a report in the Trail Times of January 24, 1949, where the idea was very well crystallized, and at the same time I must say in another newspaper report we find former President Truman had given his blessing to Senator Dill's idea. This article reads, in part:
The plan. Dill said, could be put into effect without legislation but would have to be approved by British Columbia and the international joint


commission. The commission has jurisdiction over all such Canada-United States arrangements.
Then Dill goes on to deal with certain proposals to increase the power output of the Grand Coulee dam by 500,000 to 700,000 kilowatts a year without cost to the United States government. The building of the high Arrow dam would store from 5 million to 6 million acre-feet of water which could be let down the Columbia river as needed by the generators of Grand Coulee dam in the United States.
Since that time it appears certain people have been able to get the support of officials representing governments in Canada. I have had correspondence from various people in the United States, and engineers representing private companies, to the effect that it is to our mutual advantage to see that this high Arrow dam is built. Anyway that was the genesis of the proposal first of all mentioned by former Senator Dill.
The next proposal was that of the government of British Columbia for the building of the Kaiser dam which was at a lower level and would not have created nearly as much damage. However, this was put out of court by the passage by the government of the international rivers bill, and rightly so because it would have jeopardized the whole development of the Columbia river if a private United States company had been permitted to build this dam some four miles north of Castlegar.
The latest proposal which is pressed strongly by the provincial government and which I suspect is also strongly supported by other persons unknown is for the building of the high Arrow dam four miles north of Castlegar, which if built will flood some
40,000	acres of agricultural and forest land along the Arrow lakes between Castlegar and Revelstoke and cause the inundation of some 18 communities and the loss of over 60 years work and development.
For the information of the committee and to bring this question into focus I am going to quote from various persons' remarks throughout the years to indicate their attitude to this problem. In the first instance I should like to quote Mr. Bonner of the external affairs committee of 1955, and that very famous engineer from British Columbia, Mr. Paget. During the examination of Mr. Bonner, in response to a question I asked affairs committee the question arose as to the amount of flooding which would occur in connection with the Kaiser dam. Mr. Paget, in replying to a question, said this:
There also has been a discussion of even a higher dam which would contain a great deal more water in the Arrow lakes which, if constructed, would carry a high water condition into Revelstoke, and

destroy practically the whole of the Arrow lakes economy including to the bottom lands around Arrowhead.
As hon. Mr. Bonner has mentioned, agriculture is a very important thing; and in our water resources planning we give great significance to the protection and development of agriculture-[DOT]
The extent of flooding is indicated on this map in pink; that indicates the extent of arable and available land which would be taken out of use in the proposed impounding of water which has been proposed by the national government.
The point of drawing this matter to your attention graphically in this way is to illustrate two things; First, the limited nature of the terrain which we have in British Columbia suitable and available for settlement and development is limited by our mountainous topography; and second, the care which the provincial government must exercise in examining the value of impounding waters, that is, against the areas which would otherwise be available for settlement, industry, agriculture and that sort of thing.
They of course would have been inundated if this dam went into effect. Later on Mr. Bonner, in response to a question I asked him during the committee hearings with regard to the possibility of flooding, said:
When you have narrow valleys, as we have, and where our settlements are confined to them, it becomes a matter of great moment to all of us in British Columbia when you decide to flood out a valley, because you know that thereafter, regardless of the fact that you are producing electricity you are at the same time denying available territory for future settlement, and for the dispersion of population in the province. That, in my view, is an inescapable factor for consideration by the provincial government.
Then I want to quote a telegram sent by the minister of lands, forests and mines to General McNaughton on September 18, 1954, in which the minister says:
This government cannot agree to any greater storage Arrow lakes which would flood agricultural and existing economies values hence low head dam only consideration.
That was the attitude of the British Columbia government at that time; it appears to have changed. Then I go on to quote a sentence or two from Mr. Paget when he was questioned as to flooding. He said:
Therefore we came to the proposal of a moderate storage on Arrow lakes with a view to keeping the economy of Arrow lakes still in place. When this is further analysed we find that the Murphy site can be developed with a low head, which in a critical year will justify an installation as high as 196,400 kilowatts-
Then later on he says:
To keep the record straight, because I may have misunderstood you. what I was suggesting was three million acre-feet of storage on Arrow with a low head Murphy dam with generation at the Murphy dam site. The Kaiser dam with the storage back of that dam, if constructed by Kaiser, plus storage at Mica creek, will have to be brought into being before Murphy creek is practicable.
I think those quotations indicate that at the time these gentlemen were opposed to anything more than three million acre-feet storage in the Arrow lakes because of the
Supply-Northern Affairs damage to the economy between Castlegar and Revelstoke. Then what did the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company have to say about this matter? Mr. Perry, the general manager, in a speech he was reported to have given to the chamber of commerce, said that the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company had no policy and were not concerned whether it was high or low Arrow or any Arrow at all; and the president of the West Kootenay power and Light Company said somewhat the same.
Here is an interesting aspect of the situation. You find the senior officials of West Kootenay Power and Light Company doing all they can to promote support for the high Arrow dam and giving reasons to various groups why it should be built. They do this in their private capacity as members of chambers of commerce or as members of committees appointed for that purpose. However, I think that is a very interesting state of affairs. I repeat once more the very interesting statement made by Mr. McMynn, assistant general manager of the West Kootenay Power and Light Company who is reported as follows in the Trail Times:
Mr. McMynn declared that a lot of Arrow Lakes property was "continually bothered" with flooding now, without any development on the Arrow Lakes at all.
He completely ignores all the efforts of the pioneers of the last 60 years, and all the sweat and toil that went into clearing those thousands of acres and the expenditures by the federal government on wharves and the expenditures by the provincial government on hospitals, buildings and other facilities.
"It occurred to us" he said, "that if the owners of that property could be relocated satisfactorily above high water-
What a joke on these pioneers? There is nothing above high water to cultivate.
-and the cost of relocation were paid by the authority making the development, then a great number of people inhabiting the Arrow lakes would be pleased to see that happen."
He is completely misinformed as to the attitude of a great number of people on the Arrow lakes. One finds such contradictions in statements made by officials of these large corporations. Governments are often criticized for changing their views, and the same applies to the officials of corporations. Here is an interesting one I checked at the time it was made. This is from the Nelson News. The heading reads: "No Power Lack says former district man". It reads:
British Columbia has a surplus of power and there is no need to rush to develop new sources one of the new members of the B.C. power commission said Thursday.

Supply-Northern Affairs
Frederick Arthur Lee, who began his new job on the five-man commission Thursday after 32 years with the West Kootenay Power and Light Company, said in an interview-
I may say he was the superintendent of the West Kootenay Power and Light Company.
British Columbia has to grow before it goes out and puts in new power plants.
Then he goes on to express some other ideas.
West Kootenay has a surplus of power now and there was still 750,000 horsepower which could be developed on the Pend-d'Oreille river whenever required. Kitimat also had a surplus and under a grid system this surplus could be transferred wherever needed.
Long transmission lines were no longer a problem said the former general superintendent of the West Kootenay company.
He believed development of the Columbia river was still a long way off because there had as yet been no agreement on downstream benefits.
At the present time officials of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and officials of the West Kootenay Power and Light Company are informing the public of a coming shortage of power as they expect a shortage when the new Consolidated Mining steel industry goes into operation in the Kimberley area. I judge that statement is according to the facts. However, I mention it as an expression by officials of different points of view within a few months with regard to the power situation in the interior.
First of all, I want to ask, what does General McNaughton say? There is a great deal of respect for General McNaughton in our district and I wish briefly to place on the record some highlights of his career. When you are quoting from General McNaughton you are quoting from an authority that one should pay heed to, including governments.
General the Honourable Andrew George Latta McNaughton, P.C., C.H., C.M.G., D.S.O., M.Sc., D.C.L., LL.D., P.S.C., I.D.C. soldier and engineer. Rose to high rank in the forces to be commander of the first Canadian army in the second world war after a lengthy experience in the first world war. Between the wars he served as chairman or president of several important bodies such as the atomic energy control board of Canada. He was permanent delegate from Canada to the United Nations in 1948. In 1935 he became president of the national research council, and was appointed commissioner, Canadian section international joint commission, on January 1, 1950. He is a life member of the engineering institute of Canada, 1949; honorary member Canadian institute of forestry, 1938; awarded the Sir John Kennedy medal of the engineering institute of Canada, 1940; honorary member, institution of electrical engineers,
[Mr. Herridge.l
London, 1942; honorary member, American institute of electrical engineers, New York, 1942. I have taken time to mention only a few of the highlights of General McNaugh-ton's career. Throughout the years he served as a member, adviser or chairman of many important government committees and represented Canada at the United Nations.
His qualifications are recognized from one end of Canada to the other, and they are acknowledged even in editorials in United States publications. I briefly mention this one from the Vancouver Sun of December 18, 1959 which reads, in part as follows-the heading is "All Honour to Andy":
General Andrew McNaughton has the stuff that makes great Canadians. He deserves official recognition for his outstanding victory in getting Canada a fair share of Columbia river downstream benefits.
This feat will stand as a great achievement in the history of Canadian international bargaining and as a landmark in Canadian economic development. It sets a precedent for future Canada-United States water control issues.
General McNaughton endured much uninformed and unfair political criticism on both sides of the border. But he knew his objective. He ignored all the irrelevancies.
He developed a long-headed strategy. He stuck to it-to Canada's lasting benefit.
It is true he started from a position of strength. But he suceeded in making the other side recognize reasonably quickly that it had lost the battle.
That avoided needless economic bloodshed by averting prolonged delay in coming to terms. "
McNaughton was privately determined Canada would get 50 per cent of all the U.S. power gain. And get it in value-holding electricity, not inflation-vulnerable dollars.
His masterstroke was to refuse to truckle in any way to U.S. arrogance.
He proposed diverting extra Columbia waters into the all-Canadian Fraser, thus depriving the U.S. of all benefits from Canadian control.
He had international precedent. But the Americans thought he was bluffing. Then he ordered engineering studies of this gargantuan scheme.
That might have been a big bluff. But the U.S. either overlooked it or couldn't nerve itself to call it.
Forces which preserve the Fraser for salmon could have blocked McNaughton's hydro scheme lust as they've blocked all other hydro prospects there.
As a result of the settlement, not only does Canada get 50 per cent of extra U.S. power, but the percentage is calculated on the gross increase, not the smaller net.
And in 35 to 50 years Canada can still divert Columbia waters into the Fraser if that still makes hydroelectric sense.
I commend the government for speeding up these developments and for placing the negotiations back into the hands of the Canadian section of the international joint commission to the advantage of Canada.
I now intend to quote briefly from some statements made by General McNaughton before the external affairs committee as reported in the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee dated Thursday, April

23, 1959. We were discussing proposals for the high Arrow and asking questions of General McNaughton. He had this to say:
It becomes evident, I think, that from the point of view of power production Canada would obtain no advantage whatever from flooding out of the territories along the Arrow lakes to give the increased storage represented by the high Arrow project. The advantage powerwise in that project goes entirely to the United States. The only advantage which could come to Canada would be in recompense for power produced in the United States.
Then he goes on to say, as reported on page 216:
I know that our friends from British Columbia, who worked with our engineering boards, who have been working on the committees and who in Chicago gave us an explanation of these projects have been very careful to point out the great problem involved and the economic disadvantages which would accrue to Canada from this high Arrow project.
Then from the sixth report of the proceedings dated May 18, 1960 one or two very brief quotations.
The inclusion of high Arrow in any of the plans provides no net increase in the 20-year output in Canada, but increases the critical-period average output by about 27 megawatts. In the United States, however, high Arrow adds about 164 megawatts to the critical-period average output and 196 megawatts to the 20-year average output. The net result of including high Arrow is that unit costs of the incremental power outputs are increased in Canada and decreased in the United States.
When questioned again in this respect on March 25, 1960, he said:
I would mention in reply that the introduction of the high Arrow, low down here, would put the water into storage at this point, and it would have a rather serious effect on the benefits that we would get which could be attributed to Mica.
Overnight we looked up the engineering board reports to find out just how much that benefit is.
Mr. Fleming also asked what effect that might have on the two plants below Mica on Downie creek and the Revelstoke canyon plants. I am prepared to give those figures.
With the high Arrow in place and used, the production at Mica-the attributed production with which it would be credited-is 1,322.7 million megawatts; whereas if high Arrow is left out and Mica does the regulation, then the attributed power is 1,475.2 million megawatts.
In response to the following asked by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke he said:
